Chapter 1 
Introduction 
1.1 
Purpose of and Need for Action 
This Proposed RMP is an opportunity for BLM to respond proactively in identifying the 
role of BLM land in meeting the public’s needs for open space; safety from wildfire; 
clean, abundant water for domestic, recreational, and agricultural uses; economic 
opportunities on public lands; protection and interpretation of the area’s rich historical 
heritage; and diverse, resilient habitats for enjoyment and ecosystem health.  
The PRMP will guide management of approximately 300,000 acres of surface and 
subsurface public land administered by BLM’s Folsom Field Office.  This direction will: 
1. Develop land ownership and access patterns in response to urban growth, and 
consolidate BLM’s land management responsibilities; 
2. Guide and focus recreational activities; 
3. Protect significant natural and cultural resources from human-caused damage; 
and 
4. Make recommendations regarding the management of some river corridors.   
The PRMP also addresses additional planning issues raised during scoping and the 
changed management situation that led to the initiation of this PRMP.   
BLM currently operates under the Sierra Management Framework Plan (MFP), as 
amended.  The MFP was completed in 1983 and was amended in 1988, 1993, 1995, and 
1998 to provide updated management strategies to meet:  changing resource conditions; 
new laws, rules, regulations, and BLM policies; and emerging public needs.  The most 
comprehensive amendment, adopted in 1988, focused on the adjustment of BLM’s 
ownership pattern to improve management and meet national, state, and local needs.  
Later amendments addressed management and expansion of the Red Hills ACEC (1993) 
and a land exchange involving the Ione Tertiary Oxisol Soils ACEC (1998).  The need to 
revise the MFP arose from numerous changes in circumstances and a desire to update and 
consolidate management direction for BLM lands into one document.   
Since completion of the Sierra MFP, the Sierra foothill region has experienced rapid 
population growth, which has resulted in a tremendous increase in the demand for and the 
diversity of public uses of BLM lands.  Conflicts associated with the wildland/urban 
interface (WUI) have become more frequent as the rural character of the foothills has 
transformed into a more urban environment.  In addition to issues associated with

adequately addressed in the Sierra MFP included threatened or endangered species and 
wild and scenic river eligibility and suitability.   
1.2 
Description of the Planning Area 
The planning area is BLM’s area of management responsibility (Appendix A, Maps 1a 
and 1b).  The planning area comprises all or portions of 15 counties in central California:  
Yuba, Sutter, Colusa, Nevada, Placer, El Dorado, Alpine, Amador, Calaveras, San 
Joaquin, Tuolumne, Mariposa, Sacramento, Stanislaus, and Merced (Map 1).  BLM land 
is in ten of the counties.  Four of the remaining five counties do not have BLM federal 
surface acres.  These four counties, Colusa, Sutter, San Joaquin, and Merced, are in the 
Central Valley Assessment Area.  In the remaining county (Alpine), BLM land is 
administered by the Carson City District Office in Nevada. 
Approximately 230,000 acres of BLM lands are in the planning area.  Approximately 
300,000 acres of subsurface mineral estate are administered by the field office, which 
includes approximately 72,000 acres of non-BLM surface lands where BLM manages the 
subsurface mineral estate.  The decisions in the PRMP will only apply to BLM lands and 
mineral estate in the planning area, which are referred to as the decision area.  Table 1-1 
shows the distribution of BLM land in the ten counties that are part of the decision area.

1.3 
Scoping/Planning Issues 
Planning issues are identified through public participation (scoping) and by BLM’s 
interdisciplinary planning team.  The following planning issues were determined to be the 
most important, in need of analysis, and to represent a determination of future 
management direction. 
1.3.1 
Issues Addressed in this Plan 
Issue 1:  Land Ownership Adjustment and Public Access 
Managing 1,000 isolated parcels scattered across 15 counties over a distance of 200 miles 
is inefficient.  The scattered nature of the parcels, many of which lack legal access, 
encourages trespass across private property to reach public land.  This results in law 
enforcement issues and resource damage as well as conflict between private landowners, 
the public, and BLM.  Land uses that are legal on public land can be inconsistent with the 
use and enjoyment of adjacent private property.   
There is an intense demand for access to public land that is intermixed with private land.  
Providing this access would require land ownership adjustments (exchanges, sales, or 
acquisitions) to consolidate BLM lands.  
Issue 2:  Fire and Fuels 
Fire suppression and fuels management are issues of intense public interest.  Suppression 
activities in the planning area are the responsibility of the California Department of 
Forestry and Fire Protection (CDF).  Fuels management is the responsibility of BLM. 
The increase in extensive development of rural properties for residential use adjacent to 
public land, coupled with extremely volatile fuel types and a long fire season, has created 
a very dangerous fire situation.  The fire risk is high.  The number of people at risk and 
 
1-3

Sierra Proposed RMP/Final EIS 
Chapter 1 – Introduction 
 
the value of their personal property at risk are also high.  This has resulted in greater 
demand for fuel reduction projects.  These projects need to be coordinated with local Fire 
Safe Councils, state and local fire departments, and private landowners.   
Two to three fuel reduction projects are funded per year (with 300 acres treated), while 
about 300 fuel reduction projects are needed.  This is a major concern to the public and to 
local and state agencies with fire suppression responsibilities in the planning area. 
Issue 3:  Rivers 
About every 50 miles across the planning area, along the front of the Sierra Nevada 
Mountains, a major river flows from east to west and into the Central Valley of 
California.  These rivers are:  the Yuba, the American, the Cosumnes, the Mokelumne, 
the Stanislaus, the Tuolumne, and the Merced.  Each of these rivers has two to three forks 
that are rivers in their own right.  The management of public land near these rivers is a 
major issue.  The rivers have played a historical role in the economic, social, and 
environmental development of the region.   
Portions of three rivers are designated as wild and scenic:  the North Fork American, 
Tuolumne, and Merced.  The South Yuba River has been found eligible and suitable for 
designation as a federal wild and scenic river, but to date it has not been designated.  The 
purpose of the Wild and Scenic Rivers Act is to preserve the free-flowing state of rivers 
listed in the National Wild and Scenic Rivers System or under study for inclusion in the 
system because of their outstandingly remarkable scenic, recreational, geologic, fish and 
wildlife, historic, cultural, or other similar values.  Rivers in the system are classified as 
wild, scenic, or recreational.  The act establishes requirements applicable to water 
resource projects and protects the river, or river segments, and the immediately 
surrounding land. 
One of the most significant issues in the PRMP is whether any rivers in the planning area 
are eligible and suitable for designation as wild and scenic rivers.  Studies have been 
conducted as part of the RMP process to determine whether any of the rivers possess the 
outstandingly remarkable values necessary for designation (Appendix E). 
Issue 4:  Recreation Management 
The enormous increase in population in the planning area has intensified the demand for 
recreation on public land.  Not only has demand increased, but the kinds of recreational 
activities taking place on public land have also increased, and conflicts are developing.  
Participants in off-highway vehicle (OHV) use and target shooting are finding it 
increasingly difficult to recreate where people do not object to their activities.  Noise, 
resource damage, fire hazards, and safety are issues of concern involving these activities.   
Rivers are extremely popular as swimming and water play areas, and attract hundreds of 
people on warm summer days.  Any place where a highway crosses a river over public 
land receives heavy recreational use.  Conflicts with swimmers and sun bathers occur in

areas where these activities are impacted by noise and siltation sometimes caused by 
suction dredging activities. 
Heavy demand for boating has led to congestion-related conflicts.  There is a need for 
rafting, beginning kayaking, and expert kayaking opportunities.  Rapids, lunch and 
camping areas, parking areas, and put-in and take-out locations are all seeing increased 
demand and the need for thoughtful planning and conflict resolution. 
Trails are enormously popular to a wide range of users.  There is a demand for new trail 
systems and improvements and maintenance to existing trails.  Conflicts between the 
various types of use (motorized, equestrian, mountain bikes, and pedestrians) are 
becoming more frequent. 
Hunting demand on public lands for deer, turkey, pigs, quail, band-tailed pigeons, and 
doves is high, but such activity is becoming increasingly incompatible with increased 
residential development in the planning area.   
Gold panning and suction dredging are also popular recreational pursuits.  Meetings at 
one local club average over 100 attendees.  The noise and siltation caused by dredging 
activities often cause conflict with other river users. 
Caving, geo-caching, paint ball wars, Frisbee golf, and many other forms of recreation 
take place on public land.  The issues to be resolved are how to integrate recreational 
activities within the area’s land ownership pattern in a fair and equitable manner and how 
to allow recreational use without damaging resources or adversely affecting nearby 
private landowners. 
Issue 5:  Special Area Management 
Unique and important areas, values, or resources in the planning area meet the criteria for 
protection and management under special designations.  These areas may have rare 
plants, soils, or wildlife or have special cultural, historical, visual, or recreational values.  
The designation and future management of these areas must be decided. 
1.3.2 
Issues Considered but not Further Analyzed 
The following issues raised during scoping are outside the scope of the Sierra PRMP but 
may be addressed by BLM at another time or through other means.  These issues and a 
BLM response are identified below: 
• Physical and financial maintenance of fuels reduction projects.  The 
physical aspects of maintenance regularly will be addressed by BLM’s Fire 
Management Plan and annual staff work plans.  Budgets for completing 
maintenance are controlled by Congress on an annual basis. 
• Type of rights-of-way issued.  Specifications of rights-of-way (ROWs) vary 
on a case-by-case basis.  The process and limitations of ROWs are determined 
by law and BLM policy.

• Removal of Red Hills soaproot from the sensitive species list.  BLM will 
determine outside of this planning process whether the Red Hills soaproot 
should remain on the sensitive species list.  The field office will make an

• Utilization of volunteers.  Recruitment and opportunities for volunteers is an

• Wilderness designation for the Merced River Wilderness Study Area.

Planning Criteria 
1. The Sierra RMP and EIS comply with the Federal Land Policy and 
Management Act of 1976 (FLPMA), the National Environmental Policy Act 
(NEPA), BLM planning guidelines, and other laws and regulations.  
2. The planning area has eight assessment areas, based on major watersheds. 
3. OHV routes will be designated for the planning area.

1.5 
Planning Process 
BLM’s land use planning process meets the requirements of FLPMA, which are to focus 
on the management of public lands, involve the public, and work toward BLM’s mission 
of multiple use and sustained yield.  BLM incorporates NEPA into the planning process 
to develop an EIS.  The steps in the planning process are shown in Figure 1-1. 
1.5.1 
Public Scoping 
BLM officially initiated the planning process for the Sierra RMP with publication of a 
Notice of Intent in the Federal Register on November 29, 2004.  Media releases 
requested public input and announced public scoping open houses, which were held in 
Colfax, Grass Valley, Placerville, Jackson, San Andreas, Sonora, and Mariposa between 
January 12 and March 23, 2005.   
Workshops were held on March 1, 2006, to discuss social/economic issues and concerns 
in BLM area and to increase public involvement in the development of the Sierra 
RMP/EIS.  The workshops focused on characterizing existing conditions and trends in 
local communities and the wider region that may affect and be affected by BLM’s land 
use planning decisions. 
1.5.2 
Public Comment on the Draft RMP/EIS 
The Sierra Draft RMP/EIS became available for a 90-day public comment period that 
was initiated through a Notice of Availability published in the Federal Register on 
September 15, 2006.  The formal public comment period closed on December 13, 2006.  
BLM also hosted four public meetings to encourage the public to become familiar with 
the draft RMP/EIS and share their questions and concerns:   
• October 10, 2006:  Grass Valley 
• October 18, 2006:  Mariposa 
• October 25, 2006:  Sonora 
• November 1, 2006:  Placerville

2.0 
Introduction 
This chapter describes management scenarios for the land and resources managed by 
BLM, including a “no action” alternative (Alternative A) and three “action” alternatives 
(Alternatives B, C, and D).  Alternative D is the Proposed RMP.  The alternatives 
represent a reasonable range of approaches to managing land and activities consistent 
with law, regulation, and policy.  Development of these management alternatives has 
been guided by NEPA, FLPMA, and by regulations, policy, and public input. 
The alternatives include specific actions that would guide management of the resources 
and activities on BLM land.  However, not all issues can be resolved in an RMP; some 
will require subsequent site-specific planning to determine how to reach desired 
conditions or achieve a desired result.  The allocation of lands for different uses achieved 
by this PRMP should not be considered the final determination of land use for the 
planning area.  The planning process is dynamic and uses the best available science and 
land use planning to achieve conservation of the species and communities known to be in 
jeopardy.  Technologies of the future can and are expected to alter provisions of the 
PRMP to improve upon the implementation of its objectives. 
 
This chapter starts with a discussion of how the alternatives were developed; summarizes 
the four alternatives and identifies the Proposed RMP; discusses alternatives considered 
but eliminated from detailed analysis; describes each of the four alternatives in a 
narrative form; and then lists specific proposed actions by BLM program (i.e., soil 
resources, recreation, energy and minerals, etc.).  The Executive Summary compares key 
proposals under each of the four alternatives.  Where the existing plan, described in 
Alternative A, does not provide specific guidance on issues or program areas, 
overarching laws, regulations, and policies guide management.  Alternatives B, C, and 
the Proposed RMP provide additional guidance for meeting relevant laws, regulations, 
and policy.  Input from guiding legislation/policies, public scoping, and interagency 
discussions led to alternatives that cover a relatively focused range of options.

planning area’s natural character and a variety of resource uses and management issues.

reasonable; balance resource protection with use; be responsive to issues identified by the

2.0.4 
Narrative Description of Alternatives 
Alternative A (No Action-Continues Present Management Direction) 
Alternative A is derived from examining past planning decisions and outcomes and 
extending them into the future.  The basis for this alternative is the Sierra MFP and land 
use decisions made in the absence of specific decisions or management direction 
provided by that plan.  The plan was developed in the early 1980s and is quite general, 
which is typical of land use plans of that period.  The general nature of the plan required 
many land use decisions based on an immediate interpretation of policy and management 
necessity.  Overall, the outcome of this approach has been favorable, and many initiatives 
derived from this approach have received widespread public support.  In some cases, 
BLM’s assistance was needed by various partners at local, state, and federal government 
levels and led to specific land use decisions, such as BLM’s participation in the Pine Hill 
Preserve and the Cosumnes River Preserve.   
Collaboration with local communities has been accomplished using a “community based 
planning” approach which involves public involvement in every stage of planning, from 
scoping to implementation.  This process, although lengthy, has proven very effective in 
producing plans with widespread public support.  Community based planning is very 
useful in planning for the management of the isolated and scattered public lands in the 
Sierra Nevada foothills.  Several plans have been completed using this process with great 
success.  Under all alternatives, the ‘Inimim, Round Mountain, South Fork American 
River, South Yuba River, and other community based plans would remain in effect.  The 
community based planning process would continue into the future as BLM’s primary 
land use planning tool at the community level.  
Fire suppression would continue to be a high priority.  Fuels reduction is needed 
throughout the planning area.  Approximately 300 potential fuel reduction projects have 
been proposed.  However, BLM is typically limited by funding to three to five fuels

projects per year for the foreseeable future.  BLM would continue to coordinate with  
26 fire safe councils and over 100 communities at risk. 
The existing plan calls for BLM to manage timber for production in accordance with 
Sustained Yield Unit-15.  SYU-15’s age was based on an inventory of the forestland and 
harvest calculations that are now archaic.  Thus, BLM’s management has become 
increasingly focused on responsive management, emphasizing forest health.  Since the 
mid-1980s, BLM’s timber harvest levels have varied, with highs of 2.5 million board feet 
in some years.  In recent years, however, production has dropped substantially; most 
timber sales have normally involved the salvage of timber damaged by insects, disease, 
and fire.  The existing plan allows for the harvest of 2.5 to 4 million board feet per year.  
The average salvage has been less than 250,000 board feet per year.   
The existing plan calls for BLM to increase forage production and manage grazing to 
provide 700 pounds per acre of residual mulch.  However, grazing has declined as many 
ranchers have left the livestock business.  Most grazing leases are held by individuals 
who do not depend on grazing for a central source of income; in fact, some lessees have 
no livestock.  Many of these leases are relinquished upon renewal, and this trend is likely 
to continue.  An average of four leases is relinquished each year.  Lease renewal is 
determined on a case-by-case and is based on validity of the lease, size of the lease, 
resource condition, and economic considerations of both the lessee and BLM. 
Mining claim administration for locatable minerals would continue at a level of about 
1,200 claims, with about 10 plans of operations and 20 notices filed per year.  Most plans 
of operations involve gold prospecting in underground mine workings or suction 
dredging in rivers and large creeks.  The plans are subject to environmental restrictions 
that ensure protection of significant biological and cultural resources.  Suction dredging 
in wild and scenic rivers would be allowed under approved plans as long as it does not 
impact significant biological and cultural resources or the river’s outstandingly 
remarkable values.  It is likely only a few claims would be developed into industrial 
mining operations.   
The existing plan allows mineral material sales and free use in most of the planning area.  
Most free use permits have been limited to existing pits used by local government.  
Interest in sand and gravel sales in the Yuba Goldfields would continue.  Oil and gas 
would be available for lease on 37,000 acres with high potential in the CVAA and the 
YRAA.  Lands in national wildlife refuges would not be available.  Historic development 
of federally managed oil and gas deposits in the planning area has been low and is 
expected to remain low (Appendix D, Reasonably Foreseeable Development Scenario).   
Recreation demand would continue to increase, which is not addressed in the current 
plan.  White water boating, hiking, equestrian activities, target shooting, hunting, OHV 
use, and suction dredging would be the most popular uses, with other forms of recreation 
growing in popularity and affecting public land use demands.  The demand comes from 
both private individuals and commercial organizations.  There would be increasing 
competition between users.  Under Alternative A, additional trails would be built, and 
existing trails would receive increased use.

ecosystems in the face of urban growth and residential development through protection or

2.15 
Recreation  
Under Alternatives B, C, and the Proposed RMP, BLM lands would be designated as an 
SRMA or ERMA.  SRMAs would focus on producing specific recreational opportunities.  
ERMAs would be all BLM lands outside of SRMAs.  ERMA management would be 
largely custodial.   
Terms and Definitions 
• Non-motorized Recreation:  white water rafting, hiking, backpacking, bird and 
wildlife viewing, equestrian use, environmental education, sightseeing, 
picnicking, photography, hunting, shooting, and other non-motorized activities.  
Non-motorized recreation does not include activities listed as motorized or 
mechanized recreation. 
• Mechanized Recreation:  cycling, mountain biking, hang gliding, and rock-
climbing using assistive (mechanical) devices such as bolts, ascenders, etc.   
• Motorized Recreation:  OHV use and car touring. 
The Recreation Opportunities Spectrum (ROS) identifies broad categories of recreation 
activities and experiences in the proposed SRMAs.  Identified recreation opportunities 
can be administered by managing the setting, facilities, signing, level of management 
presence/law enforcement, and types of access to these areas.  The terminology for this 
ROS has been customized to fit the scattered land pattern in the planning area’s river 
corridors.  The definitions and categories are directed toward summer, peak use, and 
water or trail-oriented activities.  Other recreation activities may be important and equally 
valued, but may not require ROS characterizations for management purposes.  Recreation 
opportunities for proposed SRMAs are organized into three major categories:

3.0 
Introduction 
As part of BLM’s land-use planning process, BLM must analyze available inventory data 
and other information to characterize the planning area, portray the current management 
situation, and identify management opportunities that respond to issues identified during 
scoping.  This analysis sets the stage for formulating a range of reasonable alternatives.  
Chapter 3 summarizes the results of this analysis undertaken by BLM staff in 2005.  This 
chapter describes characteristics and conditions of BLM lands; the status of physical and 
biological processes on these lands that affect environmental health; the condition of 
individual environmental resources such as soil, water, vegetative communities, and 
wildlife; the relative value and scarcity of these resources; and the current trends in uses 
of the lands.  This analysis of the existing management situation is, in part, the basis for 
the “no action” alternative and creates a framework from which to resolve the planning 
issues through the development of the three “action” alternatives. 
3.0.1 
Overview of the Affected Environment 
BLM is directly responsible for the management of 231,386 acres of public land scattered 
throughout ten central California counties.  Most of the acreage is in the historic Mother 
Lode region of the Sierra Nevada Range between Yuba County in the north and Mariposa 
County in the south.  
Some BLM lands, mostly along river corridors or in the Central Valley, have been 
acquired from private owners.  The scattered nature and odd shapes of BLM public lands 
in the planning area make management and boundary identification a challenge for both 
BLM and the public.  
The importance of these public lands for recreation, important habitat, and open space is 
increasing within the foothill counties as more people and businesses move to the region.  
BLM WUI is extensive and growing.  
BLM manages land with habitats typical of the lower elevations (below 4,000’) of the 
western Sierra Nevada, including annual grassland, oak woodland, chaparral, riparian, 
and mixed conifer forest.  About 25,555 acres in the planning area are managed for 
timber.  
Most BLM lands are available for recreational use by the public.  Activities such as 
hiking, picnicking, hunting, horseback riding, nature study, and camping are popular.  
Four BLM campgrounds are in the planning area:  one on the South Yuba River and three

Assessment Area, are noted for spectacular wildflower displays in the spring. 
BLM manages recreation on the following rivers:  South Yuba, North and South Forks of 
the American, Mokelumne, lower Merced, and a portion of the Tuolumne.  Permits are 
issued to private concessionaires to conduct whitewater rafting trips.  The planning area 
has one wilderness study area. 
BLM is involved in the Cosumnes River Preserve as a partner in a unique public-private 
partnership that includes The Nature Conservancy, Ducks Unlimited, California 
Department of Fish and Game, and the County of Sacramento.  The purpose of the 
Preserve is to provide waterfowl habitat on existing and former agricultural lands.  This is 
part of a coordinated federal/state effort to preserve wetlands and riparian forests.  The 
Preserve is open to the public for wildlife compatible recreation, including hiking, 
canoeing, picnicking, and nature watching.  BLM is also co-manager of the Pine Hill 
Preserve.  This multi-agency partnership established a preserve with several units from 
Salmon Falls, on the South Fork American River, to the Cameron Park Shopping Center 
area.  This preserve protects rare plants endemic to rare gabbro soils.   
The planning area contains six ACECs.  Each of these has special or unique qualities that 
require management attention.  BLM also manages three federal wild and scenic rivers 
(the North Fork American, Tuolumne, and the Merced rivers) and the state designated 
wild and scenic South Yuba River.  The ‘Inimim Forest is on San Juan Ridge in the Yuba 
River Assessment Area and is managed by BLM in cooperation with local residents. 
More detailed information about BLM’s existing management situation is discussed by 
program/resource in the rest of this chapter.  
3.0.2 
Overview of the Social Environment 
This section provides a brief overview of the prominent forces, trends, and other key 
factors that are affecting social conditions relating to management of BLM lands in the 
planning area.  Key factors include:  
• Many people from several geographical areas are affected in some way by BLM 
land and decisions.  The number of people affected is growing rapidly.  
• These people have diverse and sometimes disparate views about BLM land.  
• The diversity of public use is astounding and is expected to increase.  
Because of the rapid influx of people to the Sierra foothills that is expected to continue 
over the next several years, a detailed snapshot of current demographics in the planning 
area may not hold true in a few years.  Therefore, user groups that may be affected by 
BLM decisions in this RMP will only be described in very general terms (see below).

3.1 
Air Quality 
The planning area is primarily in the Mountain Counties Air Basin, as defined by the 
California Air Resources Board.  This air basin covers the central and northern Sierra 
Nevada Mountains, including the following counties:  Plumas, Sierra, Nevada, Central 
Placer, Western El Dorado, Amador, Calaveras, Tuolumne, and Mariposa.   
The Clean Air Act as amended in 1990 requires federal agencies to comply with all 
federal, state, and local air pollution requirements.  BLM is required to comply with the 
California State Implementation Plan for achievement of National Ambient Air Quality 
Standards for criteria pollutants.  Prevention of Significant Deterioration (PSD) goals 
guide protection of air quality and visibility in wilderness areas and national parks, and 
local Air Pollution Control Districts’ rules and regulations. 
3.1.1 
Current Condition 
Because many people commute from this area to jobs in other areas, the largest source of 
air pollutants in the basin has become motor vehicles.  Motor vehicles account for 
53 percent of oxides of nitrogen (NOx) emissions, 28 percent of reactive organic gasses 
(ROG) emissions, 36 percent of carbon monoxide (CO) emissions, and 1 percent of 
PM10 (particulate matter with an aerodynamic diameter of less than 10 µm) emissions.  
Of the criteria pollutants, portions of the Mountain Counties Air Basin violate the State 
ozone and PM10 standards (see Table 3-1 – Non-attainment Areas).

OHV recreation use contributes a minor amount of ozone to the air basin; however, OHV

BLM fire and fuels management has the potential to impact PM10 and other criteria 
pollutants.  BLM prepares smoke management plans for every prescribed burn in 
coordination with the local air quality management district to mitigate these impacts and 
ensure compliance with standards.  Wildland fires often result in a negative short-term

air quality and visibility.  EPA’s Natural Events Policy addresses events that lead to 
violations of national air quality standards.

unpaved roads and trails, contributes to PM10 within the planning area.  BLM makes an 
effort to minimize fugitive dust from construction activities and road maintenance by

3.2 
Soil Resources 
3.2.1 
Regional Geological Context 
The planning area lands are within the Western Metamorphic Belt of the Sierra Nevada 
geomorphic province.  This is a belt of steeply dipping meta-sedimentary and meta-
volcanic rocks of Paleozoic (570 to 225 million years before present (BP)) and Mesozoic 
(225 to 65 million years BP) age that lies between the granitic Sierra Nevada batholith to 
the east and overlapping sediments of the Great Valley province of central California to 
the west.  The Sierra Nevada metamorphic belt consists of northward-trending fault 
blocks that accreted to the continent by subducting activity that culminated in the Late 
Jurassic (190 to 135 million years BP).  During the Nevadan Orogeny, the sedimentary 
and volcanic rocks became highly deformed and weakly metamorphosed, and were 
intruded by plutons associated with the emplacement of the Sierra Nevada batholith.   
During the first half of the Tertiary (65 to 2 million years ago) period, river systems 
developed in the ancestral Sierra Nevada Range that formed during the Nevadan 
Orogeny.  These rivers probably originated in the highlands of this mountain range in 
western Nevada and flowed westward into a marine basin located in present day 
California’s Central Valley.  During Paleocene to Late Eocene times (ca. 65 to 40 million 
years BP), as the mountain mass underwent reduction due to extensive weathering and 
erosion, great quantities of fluvial sediments accumulated in the stream channels.  These 
channel-fill deposits, commonly called “Tertiary gravels,” accumulated in river meanders 
within extensive floodplains.  The Tertiary gravels were overlain by volcanic flows, 
including rhyolitic tuffs and andesitic breccias (with interbedded sediments) deposited 
throughout the region from the Late Eocene to the Pliocene (ca. 40 to 5 million 
years BP).   
Movements and faulting in the earth’s crust from Middle Miocene (ca. 15 million years) 
to Early Pleistocene (2 million years) caused a rapid uplift of the Sierra Nevada province 
as it tilted westward, breaking along a fault system at its eastern limit.  Thousands of feet 
of fault displacement caused stream erosion to accelerate dramatically, cutting the deeply 
incised canyons that are present today.   
3.2.2 
Resources 
Soil is a basic resource on which vegetation and, by extension, wildlife depend.  The 
hydrology of watersheds is also highly dependent on soil conditions.  If soils are 
damaged, other resources may be adversely affected and possibly destroyed.  This 
particular relationship between natural resources is important because most of the 
planning area soils are classified as moderately to highly erodible.  Variables in site slope 
and soil texture interact to determine erodibility (see below).  Sandy and silt loams on 
steep sites generally constitute the highest erosion hazard.  Soil situations of this type are 
widely scattered throughout the planning area.   
The soils of the planning area occur primarily on hilly terrain that is partially dissected by 
steep river canyons.  Roughly 80 percent of the area has slopes between 15 and

75 percent.  Thirty percent of the area is above 50 percent slope.  Rock outcrops covering 
10 to 25 percent of the land surface are common.  Some of the soils are very stony. 
The soils fall into two broad categories:  soils of the foothills and soils of the 
mountainous uplands.  These categories are, in turn, further subdivided into  
18 associations (details can be found in the county-specific soils surveys published by the 
Natural Resource Conservation Service).  The soils of the foothills are found at lower 
elevations and generally support annual grasses and forbs, with open stands of gray pine, 
oak, and shrub.  Some foothill areas have dense brush.  The soils of the mountainous 
uplands support forests of conifers and associated hardwoods, dense brush, and small 
areas of grasses and forbs. 
Most of the area’s soils developed over metasedimentary rock, coarse-grained basic and 
acidic igneous rocks, and volcanic tuff.  Depth to bedrock ranges from very shallow (less 
than 10 inches) to very deep (greater than 60 inches).  Surface textures are predominately 
loamy, while subsoil textures are loamy or clayey.  Soils reaction ranges from neutral to 
very strongly acid. 
Serpentine soils are found in some parts of the planning area.  These are erosive soils that 
have formed from highly sheared and fractured serpentine rock containing abundant 
chrysotile asbestos.  There have also been reports of tremolite and actinolite asbestos on 
lands in the planning area.  Many of these steep slopes lack soil or vegetative cover.  The 
asbestos component of these soils can become airborne when the soil is dry and a 
surface-disturbing event occurs, such as windy conditions, vehicle travel, or construction 
activity.  Exposure to asbestos from inhaling dust originating from serpentine soils is a 
concern at both federal and state levels.  Airborne asbestos can be a health hazard.  
Maximum asbestos standards have been established for the use of asbestos-bearing rock 
for road surfacing, for instance, because vehicle traffic can cause asbestos to become 
airborne.  BLM conforms to these standards for road surfacing. 
BLM manages substantial areas of ultramafic (basic) rock, some of which is asbestos 
bearing.  If any health agency advises BLM there is a health hazard associated with BLM 
lands and associated activities, appropriate warnings will be posted.  Chrysotile occurs at 
the Voorhees Asbestos Mine site 7 miles southeast of Copperopolis.  However, none of 
the ultramafic areas managed by BLM have the kind of activity that is likely to cause 
substantial amounts of asbestos to become airborne.  Only in the Red Hills is there 
substantial visitation.  There is one road in the Red Hills (see Map 6f) that is partially 
unsurfaced and available for public use.  The dominant substrate in the Red Hills is the 
ultramafic rock dunite, which does not appear to be fibrous and asbestos bearing.  The 
use of the road is largely seasonal, and speeds of travel are generally slow.  The use 
pattern does not suggest any individuals visit regularly and repeatedly.  Other ultramafic 
substrate areas have even less activity.  In sum, it seems highly unlikely that anyone 
would receive substantial exposure to naturally occurring asbestos by visiting the public 
lands of Folsom Field Office. 
The water erosion hazard for most of the area is moderate to very high.  Soils with a 
5 to 15% slope have a slight or moderate water erosion hazard rating.  Soils with a

15 to 50% slope have a moderate to high rating, while those in with a 50 to 75% slope 
have a high to very high rating.  Within each category of slope range, variations in 
erosion potential are due to factors such as soil texture, rock fragment content, organic 
matter content, and clay mineralogy.  Among the surface textures represented in the area, 
clay loams are generally the least erodible, followed by loams, sandy loams, and silt 
loams.  The more rock fragments or organic matter in the soil, the less erodible it is.  
Hydrophobic layers near the surface, which sometimes develop from exposure to 
wildfire, can make soils, particularly granitic soils, very erodible.  On any of the soils 
with a moderate or greater rating, accelerated surface runoff from winter precipitation is a 
concern, particularly where there has been off-road use of vehicles, removal or damage of 
riparian vegetation, and where there are fire breaks, dirt roads, and trails. 
In an effort to define the erosion status of soils in the area, information was gathered at 
313 sample sites on public land.  Forty-nine percent of the sites were rated as “stable.”  
Forty-seven percent evinced “slight erosion,” while the remaining 4% displayed 
“moderate erosion.”  Most sites above a 30% slope were classified as having “slight 
erosion.”  Erosion was not a critical problem at any of the sample sites, though problem 
areas are known to exist elsewhere on BLM land.  Despite the high potential for erosion 
of many of these soils, this study indicates soils are generally stable or experiencing 
slight erosion. 
Although sheet erosion occurs on soils in the planning area, erosion from channeled 
surface runoff is the greatest source of soil erosion and resulting sediment load in rivers 
and streams.  Many factors affect the degree of soil erodibility and the type of erosion.  
Rainfall intensity, slope, plant cover, and the physical and chemical properties of the soil 
affect the extent and type of erosion that occurs.  In part, high erosion rates in the 
serpentine watersheds are a natural consequence of the erodible soils formed from highly 
sheared and fractured serpentine rock containing abundant chrysotile asbestos.  Many of 
these soils are on steep slopes and are sparsely covered with vegetation.  On these barren 
slopes, runoff from winter storms can cause extensive rill and gully erosion, which 
contributes to sediment yields in stream channels. 
3.2.3 
Current Condition 
Soils found on BLM lands are currently managed with the goal of maintaining 
productivity and minimizing erosion.  Soil erosion is greatest in areas that have had 
human-related disturbances, such as road construction, domestic livestock grazing, OHV 
use, mineral extraction, and mechanized fire suppression and prevention activities.  
Where human-related disturbance is slight, soil goals have been consistently achieved. 
Moderately high to extremely high rates of soil erosion appear to be concentrated near 
motorized vehicle routes, hill climbs, fire breaks, and inner gorge areas adjacent to stream 
channels.  Road and trail maintenance, physical closure of areas of illegal vehicular use, 
and rehabilitation of fire suppression activities are actions routinely taken by BLM to 
minimize soil erosion.  Efforts also are made through regulation and permitting processes 
at the state and local governmental levels to minimize soil erosion from human-related 
disturbances.  Eroded soil that reaches streams is transported downstream during high

flows and affects downstream land and water users.  Turbidity can harm fish and wildlife 
and interferes with agricultural and municipal water systems. 
Causes of gully formation, which have been large contributors to sediment yield, include 
past practices such as livestock grazing, uncontrolled OHV use, stream diversions, and 
poorly designed or maintained roads.  Erosion on barren and vegetated slopes affects soil 
texture, fertility, and rooting depth, and can reduce infiltration, water holding capacity, 
and soil productivity.  However, because bedrock controls the depth of channels in most 
drainages in this area, gully erosion is relatively infrequent. 
3.2.4 
Trend 
Continued development on private land within the planning area is anticipated and will 
include activities that disturb the soil surface by direct displacement, compaction, and 
removal of protective vegetation and biological soil crusts.  This will result in an 
increased susceptibility to wind and water erosion.  Despite regulations and enforcement, 
some indiscriminate vehicle use off of existing roads and trails will continue.  With the 
growth of communities, the WUI will continue to expand, leading to an increase in 
activities that threaten soil integrity.

3.3 
Water Resources 
3.3.1 
Surface Water 
Unmodified surface water (rivers, creeks, streams, natural lakes, etc.) satisfied the needs 
of Californians until the Gold Rush of 1848, which spawned a huge population increase 
and an industrial and agricultural boom.  Since then, California’s population has been 
increasing steadily.  As a result, water needs have exceeded the surface water supply in 
many areas and at certain times of the year.  California currently has the highest level of 
agricultural and municipal water use in the United States.  Unmodified surface water no 
longer provides adequate water to support agricultural and urban areas.  To resolve this 
problem, almost all of California’s usable surface water is stored in approximately 
1,200 federal, state, and local reservoirs and is transported throughout the state by a 
network of aqueducts.  There are numerous reservoirs in the Sierra Nevada region, 
particularly the foothills.  According to the state’s water plan, more than 75% of available 
surface water is stored and exported to areas outside of the Sierras and foothills.  
Approximately 45 significant reservoirs are in the planning area.  BLM manages public 
land around some of these reservoirs including New Melones, Don Pedro, and McClure 
reservoirs.  Approximately 30 significant reservoirs are in the mountains above BLM 
lands which feed, and therefore impact through flow regulation, etc., the rivers and 
streams managed by BLM.  Activities on private land such as water diversions, 
viticulture, agriculture, logging, etc., above BLM lands also affect surface waters 
managed by BLM.  Historic mining activities also affect water quality.  Mercury has been 
found in a number of rivers and streams managed by BLM.  Other chemicals found in the 
waters managed by BLM include zinc, copper, arsenic, Diazinon (an insecticide), and 
pesticide residues.  The State Water Resources Board defines beneficial uses critical to 
water quality management, including potential and existing beneficial uses for each river 
segment.  These uses are municipal and domestic, agricultural, industrial, recreation, 
habitat, fish and wildlife migration, and fish spawning.  Although beneficial uses are not 
met on all reaches, none of these deficiencies result from BLM management.  
BLM manages approximately 250 miles of perennial streams and rivers.  Of these, 
90.5 miles have been assessed to determine if their riparian areas are in Proper 
Functioning Condition.  According to Riparian Area Management:  Process for 
Assessing Proper Functioning Condition (BLM Manual TR 1737-9 1993): 
Riparian-wetland areas are functioning properly when adequate 
vegetation, landform, or large woody debris is present to dissipate stream 
energy associated with high waterflows, thereby reducing erosion and 
improving water quality; filter sediment, capture bedload, and aid 
floodplain development; improve flood-water retention and ground-water 
recharge; develop root masses that stabilize stream banks against cutting 
action; develop diverse ponding and channel characteristics to provide the 
habitat and the water depth, duration, and temperature necessary for fish 
production, waterfowl breeding, and other uses; and support greater

Sacramento Delta. 
Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) Licensing 
The available high-value hydroelectric resources in the planning area have largely been 
developed.  Opportunities for smaller hydro projects are still available, especially in areas 
where high energy streams, road access, and existing power transmission lines are all in 
the same vicinity.  The planning area is typical of the western Sierra where large volumes 
of water runoff and mountainous terrain provide head (elevational differences) to run 
generators and furnish reservoirs.  California has high potential for producing 
hydroelectric power and has more applications filed with FERC than any other state.   
BLM does not actively supply or promote hydro development.  However, these resources 
are, by law, available for development as long as they are consistent with the mission of 
BLM, comply with the Sierra RMP, and contain provisions for the protection of natural 
resources.  FERC controls licensing of hydro resources for the nation.  All projects on 
public lands must have either a license or exemption from licensing by FERC before 
BLM can grant authorizations to construct facilities.  Hydro development is usually 
compatible with land use direction for the Folsom Field Office and can be accommodated 
as proposed.  However, in some areas, hydro development can conflict with other land 
uses or resource objectives such as in wilderness study areas, ACECs and other specially 
designated areas.  In these cases, BLM can recommend FERC deny a request for a 
license and/or determine mitigation that would help offset resource impacts caused by a 
hydro project.

3.4 
Vegetative Communities  
Vegetative communities in the planning area are generally characterized by conifer forest 
in the higher elevations, chaparral and live oak woodlands in the mid-to-lower elevations, 
eventually transitioning into blue oak woodland/savannah and grassland in the lowest 
elevations.  Riparian areas traverse the entire length of the planning area along river 
corridors.  The area’s most uncommon vegetative communities occur in association with 
rare soil types:  gabbro, serpentine, and soils associated with the Ione Formation.  Rare 
plants are often found in association with these soil types, including some plant species 
endemic to these soils.  More information about these unique soil types and the rare 
plants associated with them can be found in  
Section 3.19, “Special Designations.”  
3.4.1 
Invasive Non-native Species 
Invasive non-native species are present on many BLM parcels in the planning area.  
According to “Pulling Together:  National Strategy for Invasive Plant Management,” 
noxious weeds are already present on over 100 million acres throughout the United States 
(on both public and private lands), and this number increases by approximately 3 million 
acres each year.  Noxious weeds threaten agricultural production, biodiversity, and native 
habitats.  The habitat of over 60 percent of special status species is threatened by weeds.   
Noxious weed control is estimated to cost between $3.6 and $5.4 billion annually across 
the United States.  Within the planning area, BLM staff document all noxious weed 
populations found when conducting field activities.  BLM prioritizes areas most in need 
of weed treatments based on several factors, including whether the weeds are threatening 
a special status plant or animal or a unique area, if the infestation occurs in a recreation 
public use area, the size of the infestation (smaller populations are more time- and cost-
efficient to target), if it is a new infestation (new infestations are easier to eradicate), if 
the budget allows for weed control, and the most appropriate treatment type for the 
specific infestation.  Infestations are currently treated in the Red Hills ACEC, Merced 
River Campgrounds, Cosumnes River Preserve, Pine Hill Preserve, Dave Moore Nature 
Area, Greenwood Creek, and the Mokelumne River along Electra Road.  Also surveyed 
and treated (if necessary) are new infestations as a result of firefighting.  In addition, a 
weed management plan has been developed for the Cosumnes River Preserve, and a draft 
strategy has been developed for the Pine Hill Preserve.  BLM is involved with the 
Amador County Weed Group, El Dorado County Weed Group, Tuolumne Calaveras 
Central Sierra Partners against Weeds, Nevada/Placer Weed Management Area, Southern 
and Central Sierra Noxious Weed Alliance, and the California Invasive Plant Council.  
Some of the most troublesome weeds include yellow star thistle, scotchbroom, goat grass, 
and rush skeleton weed.  These weeds have received the most management attention by 
BLM and its partners.   
3.4.2 
Conifer Forest 
The conifer forest is an assemblage of conifer and hardwood species that generally forms 
a multilayered forest and occurs in the planning area at elevations from 2,500’ to

and California black oak are the dominant species.  This vegetative community occurs on 
approximately 54,591 acres throughout the planning area.  A mature forest will have trees 
100-200’ tall and 30-40” diameter at breast height.  These stands will have fuel loadings 
of 40-80 tons per acre.  Mountain misery, deerbrush, white leaf and mewukka

over 100 species of grasses, forbs, and shrubs contribute to the flora of the conifer

3.4.3 
Blue Oak Savannah/Woodland 
Blue oak woodlands mixed with gray pine tend to ring the Central Valley, ranging from 
elevations of 500-3,000’.  This vegetation type covers about 13,266 acres in the planning 
area.  Blue oak and gray pines typically comprise the overstory.  The oaks rarely exceed 
50’ tall; the pine rarely exceed 100’ high.  Interior live oak and California buckeye are 
common, and the entire community is often accompanied by large areas of annual 
grassland.  More than 300 species of wildlife use oak woodlands for breeding, feeding, 
and cover.   
3.4.4 
Live Oak Woodland 
Live oak woodlands are scattered throughout California and are mostly found west of the 
Sierra Nevada at 300-9,000’ elevation.  This vegetation type covers approximately 
32,855 acres in the planning area.  Live oak dominates the overstory, with some scattered 
knobcone pine and foothill pine.  The understory can be made up of woody shrubs, 
annual grassland, or a combination of both.  More than 300 species of wildlife use oak 
woodlands for breeding, feeding, and cover.  Scrub jays, Steller’s jays, woodpeckers, 
wild turkey, deer, gray squirrels, and other species feed on acorns produced by the oaks.  
3.4.5 
Chaparral 
In the lower elevations, chaparral dominates.  This is the most abundant vegetative 
community in the area that BLM manages, comprising of about 78,344 acres.  There are a 
large number of plants in this vegetation type.  Up to 240 species of woody plants have 
been identified in mixed chaparral.  This vegetation type tends to be dominated by shrubs 
with heavy, thick, cutinized evergreen leaves, such as scrub oak, manzanita, poison oak, 
and chamise.  This vegetation is fire adapted.  Dominant plants tend to sprout back from 
root crowns.  Many of the large and destructive wildfires in California occur in this 
vegetation type. 
Chaparral provides habitat for a wide variety of wildlife.  Deer make extensive use of 
chaparral, as do a large number of rodents.  A diversity of birds makes use of the seeds, 
fruits, insects, and protection from predators offered by the chaparral.  A large number of 
the special status plants occur in this habitat type as well.

3.4.6 
Annual Grassland 
Annual grassland is mixed somewhat with the other vegetation types, especially oak and 
chaparral communities.  Grasslands are often found on south and west aspects.  This 
vegetative community covers approximately 10,195 acres of BLM lands.  These annual 
grasses germinate with fall rains and grow slowly during the cool season until 
temperatures increase and cause rapid growth.  Introduced species dominate the flora.  
Wild oats, soft chess, ripgut brome, and foxtail are the most common grasses, and filaree 
and turkey mullein are the common forbs.  Productive sites produce up to 2 tons of 
herbage per acre. 
Grasslands provide wildlife foraging areas, but many species require other habitat 
features such as cliffs, caves, ponds, or areas with woody vegetation for breeding, resting, 
or escape cover.  Western fence lizards, garter snakes, and rattlesnakes are common.  
Mammals found in grasslands include the black-tailed jackrabbit, California ground 
squirrel, western harvest mouse, badger, and coyote.  Birds include burrowing owls, 
short-eared owl, horned lark, western meadowlark, turkey vulture, northern harrier, 
American kestrel, white-tailed kite, and prairie falcon. 
3.4.7 
Riparian Areas 
Riparian areas are common throughout the planning area along rivers and streams.  
Riparian areas sometimes have an overstory of cottonwood, California sycamore, or 
valley oak 50 to 80 feet high.  Whether or not this taller canopy is present, a lower 
canopy is often present with white alder, red willow, and Oregon ash as the dominant 
species.  The understory has a shrub layer with willows, buttonwillow, wild grape, 
Himalayan blackberry, and poison oak.  A final herbaceous layer of sedges, rushes, and 
grasses is usually present.  BLM manages approximately 250 miles of perennial rivers 
and streams and associated riparian habitat. 
Riparian areas are very important to wildlife for food, escape cover, migration routes, 
nesting cover, and dispersal corridors.  Various studies have found that 50 amphibians 
and reptiles, 147 bird species, and 55 species of mammals use the riparian areas.  Some 
are year-round residents, while others use riparian habitat for specialized purposes during 
their life cycles.

3.5 
Fish and Wildlife 
BLM has primary responsibility for the management of habitats in the planning area.  
CDFG manages species in cooperation with BLM.  Due to this management overlap, 
BLM and CDFG coordinate many activities.  BLM’s objective has been to maintain, 
protect, and enhance the density and diversity of native fish and wildlife. 
The diverse fish and wildlife resources in the planning area are an essential part of 
healthy ecological systems and provide significant recreational values.  Consumptive 
recreational uses include fishing and hunting (big game, small game, and upland game 
birds).  Fishing and hunting regulations are established and enforced by CDFG.  Non-
consumptive uses include wildlife viewing, bird watching, and catch and release fishing. 
Wildlife species have interrelationships which link species on a landscape to each other 
and to specific habitats.  Therefore, conservation measures for one species or habitat may 
be linked to conservation of an entire assemblage of wildlife species and, in some cases, 
landscapes. 
Species found on BLM land in the planning area are representative of Sierra Nevada 
foothills and Sacramento Valley flora and fauna.  Habitats of importance for wildlife and 
fish reflect the diversity of the area.  Some species are habitat generalists, occurring in a 
variety of habitat types, while other species are habitat specialists and occur in single 
habitat types.   
The tremendous geologic, topographic, and climatic diversity of California creates a 
correspondingly high level of plant and animal diversity.  However, habitat loss, 
fragmentation, or alteration threatens this diversity.  Causes include habitat conversion 
(to urban areas, agricultural lands, and vineyards), urban infrastructure such as roads and 
utility corridors, logging (roads, landings, and open areas after harvest), land ownership 
patterns (landscape fragmentation), altered fire occurrence, streambed alterations, 
invasive plants, grazing, and degradation due to recreation (OHV use, target shooting, 
hiking, bicycling, equestrian use, and other activities), and historical mining.

Rivers and streams in the planning area tend to be transitional areas, where cold and 
warm water fisheries meet.  BLM land is typically located on river reaches above 
dams/reservoirs in the 1,000 to 3,500 foot elevation.  Water temperatures are almost 
entirely dependent on dam releases, which have a direct impact on the type of fish 
present.  Reservoirs and the reaches just above the reservoirs can typically be classified 
as warm water fisheries.  Farther above, temperature regimes become more influenced by 
snowmelt and other natural factors and less influenced by dams.  This is where cold water 
fisheries would likely be located.  Reaches managed by BLM tend to be transitional areas

that cannot be clearly identified as warm or cold water fisheries, and the exact point 
where the change takes place is not always definable.  The Cosumnes River is not 
dammed, but it has transitional characteristics due to natural physical barriers and 
extremely low flows in lower reaches.  
During fall and winter, all of the rivers support salmon and steelhead runs, with fish 
spawning in gravels below physical barriers or at hatcheries.  BLM controls very little 
land in these reaches with the exception of the Cosumnes and Yuba Rivers.   
CDFG stocks numerous reservoirs throughout the area and ponds near BLM lands may 
be stocked by private landowners.  Stocked fish can swim upstream into areas managed 
by BLM which may introduce disease or large populations of undesirable fish species.   
Anadromous Fish  
Sedimentation of creeks, streams, and tributaries pose one of the biggest threats to 
anadromous fish.  Fine sediments reduce reproductive success as they settle into the 
substrate.  Refuge pools important for gonad maturation in spring-run Chinook are filled 
in, adults become less efficient at building redds, salmon eggs are buried or suffocated, 
and fry can be trapped before emergence.  As sedimentation increases, temperatures also 
increase, which can shift spawning, incubation, and emergence times, slow the growth 
process of fry, and shift the timing of migration to the ocean.  If temperatures increase 
significantly over time, reproduction may stop completely.  Migration routes with 
shallow portions may become filled in over time, preventing the salmon and steelhead 
from reaching their spawning areas.   
Fine sediments may also increase gill abrasion.  Invertebrates and aquatic insects become 
less productive, reducing the amount of food available for salmon and steelhead.  Road 
networks are responsible for much of the sedimentation.  Activities such as logging, 
agriculture, and grazing near streams and rivers can increase the likelihood of 
sedimentation.  Mining may also increase the sediment load and produce large 
concentrations of fines.  Reduction of cover and large woody debris also pose a threat to 
the survival of salmon and steelhead.  Cover provides shelter from predators, shade, and 
refugia from high- or fast-flows events.  Cover also traps sediments, aids in bank and 
channel stability, and creates such channel characteristics as back eddies, side channels, 
and pools.  Grazing near stream edges reduces vegetative cover. 
Dams are one of the biggest threats to anadromous fish by blocking migration routes.  
The Cosumnes River is the only undammed river in the planning area.  Timing and 
amount of dam releases should accommodate downstream water temperature and velocity 
requirements for fish.  Adverse impacts can include:  (1) fish blockage and mortality due 
to dams, diversion structures, turbines, spillways, and waterways; (2) alteration of stream 
and riverine habitats, natural lakes, riparian areas, and wetlands by inundation, 
dewatering, channelization, and filling; (3) changes in water quality, including sediment 
transport, dissolved oxygen, and water temperature; (4) alteration of flow regimes; and 
(5) fluctuating instream flows which create unstable habitat, degrade water quality, and

Mule Deer 
BLM manages lands in 12 CDFG Deer Management Units:  Camp Beale, Placerville, 
Mariposa, Salt Springs, Railroad Flat, Grizzly Flat, Nevada City, Blue Canyon, 
Yosemite, Tuolumne, Stanislaus, and the Sacramento Valley.  The foothills provide

winter range for many of the deer herds.  As the foothill region becomes more populated 
by humans, often leading to habitat conversion and degradation, BLM lands become 
exceedingly important to the survival of the deer herds.  Two subspecies of mule deer 
occur in the planning area:  California mule deer (Odocoileus hemionus californicus) and 
Columbian black-tailed deer (O. hemionus columbianus).  The two subspecies interbreed, 
leading to large numbers of deer that exhibit characteristics of both subspecies.  
Presently, chronic wasting disease (CWD) or other debilitating illnesses are not known to 
affect herds in California.  As of March 2004, CDFG has collected more than 1,300 tissue 
specimens throughout California, all of which tested negative for CWD.  
Habitat Requirements 
The planning area has migratory and non-migratory (resident) herds.  Resident herds 
occupy blue oak, chaparral, and annual grassland habitats, which provide year-round 
forage and cover.  Oak woodlands contain a variety of oak species, including blue and 
valley oak, and several types of live oak.  Understory vegetation in oak woodlands is 
comprised mainly of annual grasses and forbs.  Resident deer also tend to occupy urban 
areas where homes are on fairly large parcels.  In these areas, deer have enough open 
space for cover and forage, but they also forage in landscaped areas where homeowners 
water the vegetation, keeping it green year-round.  
Migratory deer herds use the planning area for wintering.  Intermediate and summer 
ranges tend to be above 4,500 feet, outside the planning area.  Winter range is comprised 
of mixed conifer with primarily mountain misery in the understory, montane chaparral 
with manzanita and a variety of ceanothus species, oak woodlands with patches of brushy 
areas, grassy areas, some conifers, and annual grasslands.  Deer begin migrating to the 
winter ranges when the first significant snow occurs (typically during December).  The 
migration may take up to three months.  They tend to remain in the winter range until 
spring, typically beginning the migration back to the summer range in March. 
Riparian areas along streams that contain willows and wild rose are particularly important 
components of deer habitat in chaparral and oak woodlands.  Riparian areas, which 
provide water, succulent forage, thermal and fawning cover, and migratory routes, are 
important to both resident and migratory deer.   
Population Trend 
BLM lands in the planning area are in four Deer Management Zones:  D-3, D-4, D-5, and 
D-6.  Deer populations in these zones are stable or declining.  CDFG biologists believe 
that long-term declines in habitat condition, starting in the 1930s and continuing today, 
are largely responsible for the decline.  Lack of habitat disturbance, especially from fire, 
has decreased habitat value for deer and other wildlife in much of the state’s forested 
areas.  Deer and numerous other species thrive on early successional vegetation that 
grows back in the first few years after fire.  Without periodic fire, the habitat becomes old 
or “decadent” and is unable to support wildlife populations as it has in the past.  Indirect

Habitat Conditions 
Vegetation is varied in Zones D-3 through D-6.  BLM lands are low elevation (below 
4,000 feet) and provide oak woodland, chaparral, hardwood, and hardwood conifer 
habitats.  Above 4,000 feet, deer habitat is comprised of aspen, dense conifer, and alpine 
habitats.  Generally speaking, deer populations in these areas respond favorably to 
vegetation disturbance that enhances brush species (wildfire and timber harvesting).  The 
deer population in Zone D-3 is stable to declining; populations in Zones D-4 and D-5 are 
stable to slightly declining.  Population declines are due to fire suppression which results 
in decadent vegetation, and weather events such as drought that limit forage production.  
The deer population in Zone D-6, however, is stable to increasing.  Fawn survival in this 
area has been good for the past several years.  
Feral Pigs 
Pigs (Sus scrofa) are not native to North America and did not exist in California before 
the early 1700s.  Spanish and Russian explorers and settlers introduced domestic pigs to 
California and allowed them to forage freely.  Feral pigs now exist in 56 of the state’s 
58 counties, and their numbers continue to increase.   
Prior to the mid-1950s, feral pigs were unclassified under state law.  During this period, 
feral pigs could be killed with no restrictions.  In 1957, the state legislature designated the 
feral pig as a game mammal.  Although CDFG has not established specific herd units or a 
designated hunting season for feral pigs in California, pig hunters are required to 
purchase feral pig tags. 
Feral pigs are found in many habitats as long as water and some cover are present.  Pig 
habitat in the planning area includes oak woodlands, chaparral, riparian, and open 
grasslands.  They are most abundant in oak woodlands interspersed with grasslands.  The 
largest concentration of feral pigs in the planning area is in the MRAA.  
Cougars (Mountain Lions) 
The cougar (Felis concolor) is native and is North America’s largest cat.  Its status in 
California evolved from that of “bountied predator” between 1907 and 1963, to “game 
mammal” in 1969, to “special protected mammal” in 1990.  Today’s population estimate 
ranges between 4,000-6,000 animals.  
Mountain lions are found in many different types of habitats, including oak woodland, 
pine, fir, annual and perennial grasslands, chaparral, and riparian.  It is the largest 
carnivore in the planning area and requires large core habitat areas, abundant prey, and 
habitat connectivity.  They generally are most abundant in areas with plentiful deer.  An 
adult male’s home range often spans over 100 square miles (20 to 60 square miles for 
females).  Urbanization threatens mountain lion populations in California, which are

Wild Turkey 
Wild Turkey (Meleagris gallopavo) populations have become an established part of 
much of California’s mixed pine-oak woodlands resulting from numerous introductions, 
the first of which was reported in 1877.  Current population estimates for wild turkeys in 
California place the population at 242,000.  Turkeys are an important game bird, valued 
by hunters and other wildlife enthusiasts. Turkey hunting is a growing sport in California. 
Suitable wild turkey habitat contains a combination of two key components:  (1) trees for 
food, escape cover, and roosting sites; and (2) grasslands which allow turkeys to forage 
while avoiding predation.  Lateral cover, associated with nest selection, is commonly 
provided by shrubs, herbaceous vegetation, and woody debris.  Water is also an important 
habitat component.  
Upland Game Birds 
BLM lands provide important habitats for upland game birds.  The California or valley 
quail (Callipepla californica) is associated with a combination of brushy vegetation, 
woodlands, canyons, foothills, and more open grassy habitat with some water.  The ring-
necked pheasant (Phasianus colchicus) is associated with grasslands, farmlands, and 
marshes.  The mourning dove (Zenaida macroura) occupies a variety of habitats, 
including farmlands, urban areas, woodlands, and grasslands.  The band-tailed pigeon 
(Columba fasciata) prefers oak and oak-conifer woodlands near water such as seeps and 
mineral springs. 
Small Game, Non-Game, and Fur-Bearing Mammals 
BLM manages habitat for small game, non-game, and fur-bearing mammals throughout 
the planning area.  Small game includes desert cottontail (Sylvilagus auduboni), brush 
rabbit (Sylvilagus bachmani), blacktailed jackrabbit (Lepus californicus), and western 
gray squirrel (Sciurus griseus).  Non-game species are bobcat (Lynx rufus), coyote (Canis 
latrans), several bat species, and California ground squirrel (Citellus beecheyi).  Fur-
bearing species include gray fox (Urocyon cineroargenteus) and raccoon (Procyon lotor). 
Habitat condition (excellent, good, fair, and poor) for these species are summarized in 
Table 3-4.  These characterizations reflect vegetation conditions, habitat fragmentation or 
density of intrusions, and conflicts with competing resource issues as indicated by 
population levels.  Applicable elements are footnoted for each condition class.

Raptors 
BLM lands include considerable raptor habitat for bald eagle, golden eagle, red-tailed 
hawk, red-shouldered hawk, rough-legged hawk, Cooper’s hawk, Swainson’s hawk, 
ferruginous hawk, northern goshawk, sharp-shinned hawk, northern harrier, merlin, 
prairie falcon, peregrine falcon, American kestrel, short-eared owl, long-eared owl, 
spotted owl, flammulated owl, great gray owl, western screech owl, great horned owl, 
burrowing owl, and osprey.  Threats to raptors include poisoning, vehicle collisions, 
habitat loss, illegal hunting, illegal trading and egg collecting, power lines and towers, 
falconry, a reduced prey base, and disturbed nesting/roosting sites.  Adult raptors have 
few predators and may live for 20 to 30 years.  Similar to other long-lived species, raptors 
have a slow breeding rate and a high mortality rate among young birds.  Approximately 
25% of raptors survive their first year, and only half of these will reach maturity and raise 
their own young.  Reduced adult survivorship due to the above-mentioned causes has 
resulted in declining populations. 
Migratory Birds 
BLM lands in the planning area contain habitat for many species of migratory birds.  The 
Migratory Bird Treaty Act of 1918, as amended, implemented the 1916 Convention 
between the U.S. and Great Britain (for Canada) for the protection of migratory birds.  
Later amendments implemented treaties between the U.S. and Mexico, the U.S. and 
Japan, and the U.S. and the Soviet Union (now Russia).  Specific provisions in the statute 
include a federal prohibition, unless permitted by regulations, to:  “pursue, hunt, take, 
capture, kill, attempt to take, capture or kill, possess, offer for sale, sell, offer to purchase, 
purchase, deliver for shipment, ship, cause to be shipped, deliver for transportation, 
transport, cause to be transported, carry, or cause to be carried by any means whatever, 
receive for shipment, transportation or carriage, or export, at any time, or in any manner,

migratory birds…or any part, nest, or egg of any such bird.” (16 U.S.C. 703).   
Threats include habitat loss, fragmentation and degradation, and increased mortality due 
to communication towers, powerlines, and wind developments.  Species on the USFWS 
Migratory Nongame Birds of Management Concern list that occur in the planning area

hummingbird, northern flicker, and tri-colored blackbird.   
Amphibians 
In the U.S., there are 21 amphibians classified as endangered or threatened and 11 species 
waiting to be listed according to the USFWS Division of Environmental Quality 
(http://contaminants.fws.gov/Issues/Amphibians.cfm, 2005).  Overall frog and 
salamander numbers are declining, and the causes have not been determined.  Habitat 
loss, degradation, urbanization, pollution, disease, pesticide drift, and herbicide runoff 
into California’s waters have been identified as potential causes for the decline.  The 
federally threatened California red-legged frog occurs in the planning area, and its 
recovery plan was finalized by the USFWS in 2002.  The foothill yellow-legged frog, 
limestone salamander, and western spadefoot (three sensitive species), and more common 
species, which include the pacific chorus frog and the California newt, also occur on 
BLM lands. 
Reptiles 
More than 20 reptile species occur in the planning area.  The western pond turtle is the 
only turtle species found in the area.  These rare turtles occur in lakes, rivers, and 
perennial streams.  The western fence lizard is the most common lizard in the planning 
area and occupies a variety of habitats.  Skinks and alligator lizards are also fairly 
common.  The California horned lizard, a BLM sensitive species, is only known at a few 
sites in the planning area.  This lizard occurs in grasslands and chaparral.  It is threatened 
by habitat loss and pesticides.  Gopher snakes, garter snakes, and the western rattlesnake 
are the area’s most common snakes.

Special Status Species 
Special status species include threatened, endangered, proposed, or candidate species for 
federal listing as well as BLM sensitive, state listed threatened or endangered species, 
California Native Plant Society List 1B, and federal/state sensitive plant species.  BLM 
sensitive species, CDFG local species of concern, and USFWS species of concern will 
hereafter be referred to as ‘sensitive species’ for ease of reference.  Candidate species are 
managed to prevent federal listing.  The restricted distributions, specialized habitat 
requirements, and population pressures (human-induced and natural) facing special status 
species contribute to a high potential for extinction; thus, their populations are of 
conservation interest.   
“Rare” is not an official BLM category, but the term is used in this document to mean 
species that are uncommon and worthy of special management attention but do not fit 
BLM’s definition of special status species.  Examples include:  species with only one or a 
few populations in the region but are more common elsewhere; newly discovered species 
whose extent are unknown; and genotypes whose taxonomic status are yet to be 
determined. 
Section 7 of the ESA, as amended, directs federal agencies to ensure actions authorized, 
funded, or carried out are not likely to jeopardize the continued existence of any 
threatened or endangered species or result in the destruction or adverse modification of 
their important habitats.  The ESA mandates agencies to consult when actions may affect 
listed species or important habitat and to confer with the appropriate Secretary whenever 
an action is likely to jeopardize the continued existence of any species proposed for 
listing as threatened or endangered, or whenever an action might result in adverse 
modification of important habitat proposed for listing (50 CFR 402).  According to BLM 
manual 6840, all non-listed special status species are to be managed so that “actions 
authorized, funded, or carried out by BLM do not contribute to the need for the species to 
become listed.”  This includes sensitive species as well as candidate species.  Tables 3-5 
and 3-6 list special status plants and animals that occur or have potential habitat on BLM

3.7 
Wildland Fire Ecology and Management  
The planning area is characterized by extremely volatile vegetation types and an 
unusually long fire season.  Private and public lands intermingle, and many of the private 
lands contain residences.  The planning area has a history of large fires resulting in 
considerable property loss.  According to public input, wildfire risk and fuels 
management comprise two of the most important issues to be addressed in this plan. 
The public has become very active in fire and fuel issues.  There are now 26 fire safe 
councils in the planning area, each devoted to making their community safe.  While the 
public demand for action is high, BLM’s ability to reduce fuels has been limited in large 
part by funding.  Though there are more than 100 communities at risk in the planning 
area, only two fuel hazard reduction projects were implemented by BLM in 2004/2005. 
The Folsom Field Office fire management program is directed by a Fire Management 
Plan (FMP) which is a strategic document for wildland fire management, fire-damaged 
ecosystem restoration, and hazardous fuels treatments in the planning area.  Direction for 
the FMP is derived from the broad guidance provided through this RMP. Any new 
guidance established in revisions to this RMP could lead to the revision of the FMP.

Fire and fuels have been affected by active and passive management since prehistoric 
times.  Vegetation and fuel type are two primary descriptors of fire and fuel resources.  
Fuel in the natural environment includes live vegetation and materials such as dead 
branches, leaves, needles, seeds, and cones.  These fuels provide the structure that, under 
appropriate conditions, supports fire across the landscape.  Vegetation and fuel are 
affected by other factors such as precipitation, temperature, soils, and seasonal 
fluctuations.

intensity, and seasonality in a given ecosystem. Fire regimes have been classified into 
five groups as summarized below:
