• Negligible – the effect is at the lower level of detection; change would be 
difficult to measure. 
• Minor – the effect is slight but detectable; there would be a small change. 
• Moderate – the effect is readily apparent; there would be a measurable change 
that could result in small but permanent change. 
• Major – the effect is large; there would be a highly noticeable, long-term, or 
permanent measurable change. 
• Localized – the effect occurs at a specific site or within a known boundary. 
• Short term – the effect occurs only for a short time after implementation of a 
management action. 
• Long term – the effect occurs for an extended period after implementation of a 
management action. 
• Direct – an effect that occurs as a result of actions on the resource being 
addressed.  
• Indirect – an effect that occurs as a result of actions on other resources. 
Cumulative Impacts 
Cumulative impacts are defined as follows (40 CFR 1508.7): 
The impact on the environment which results from the incremental impact 
of the action when added to past, present, or reasonably foreseeable 
future actions, regardless of what agency or person undertakes such 
actions.  Cumulative impacts can result from individually minor but 
collectively significant actions taking place over a period of time.  
Cumulative impacts can result from similar projects or actions, as well as 
projects or actions that have similar impacts.  
Cumulative impacts include those that occur on resources or lands outside the planning 
area or outside of BLM jurisdiction as a result of BLM actions inside the planning area.  
The time frame for the cumulative impacts analysis begins at the time the RMP would 
take effect and extends for 15 to 20 years.  Cumulative impacts can also result from non-
BLM actions on adjacent (non-BLM) land.  
4.0.3 
Incomplete or Unavailable Information 
Impacts are quantified where possible.  Impacts are sometimes described using ranges of 
potential impacts or in qualitative terms.  In the absence of quantitative data, impacts are 
described based on the professional judgment of the interdisciplinary team of technical

thus reduce the wildfire hazard.  Each air district has specific regulations regarding 
required plans and permits and conditions for prescribed burning.  Before implementing a

4.2.1 
Introduction

• Manage soil so the biological and physical characteristics are appropriate to

4.2.2 
Impacts of the Soil Resources Program’s Proposed Actions on 
Soils 
BLM manages a wide range of soils, including rare soils.  The proposed actions would 
have long-term benefits to soils by reducing erosion, limiting the transport of sediment 
into streams, and increasing vegetative health.  Preventing disturbance and compaction 
can prevent soil degradation.  If disturbance occurs, conservation of surface soils by 
stockpiling topsoil and reducing soil erosion can mitigate the adverse effects of the 
disturbance.  Revegetation is a very effective soil stabilization tool.  These best 
management practices generally reduce adverse impacts of disturbance on soils to 
acceptable levels.  
Under Alternative A, BLM would adopt the practices of the current management plan, 
which does not specifically address soil resources.  BLM would continue to follow the 
latest BLM policy concerning ecosystem management (e.g., BLM’s Rangeland Health 
Standards and Guidelines for California and Northwestern Nevada) which provide 
general guidance for soil conservation.  Overall, the impacts could be adverse, but 
probably minor.  Soil resource goals and actions proposed under Alternatives B, C, and 
the Proposed RMP would be more beneficial to soil management because they are more 
proactive.     
Alternatives B, C, and the Proposed RMP would stabilize soil and control erosion on 
Truro Mine Road, Rewinkle Road, and Weber Creek Road (ARAA) and in the Bald 
Mountain parcel (TRAA).  These actions would result in long-term, localized benefits to 
soils.  In addition, these actions would result in secondary beneficial impacts on water 
quality, vegetation, and road stability.  Also beneficial is the continued protection of the 
soils in the Ione Tertiary Oxisol Soils ACEC.   
4.2.3 
Impacts of Other BLM Programs’ Proposed Actions on Soils  
Soil quality and productivity can be degraded by activities such as high-impact 
recreational use, livestock grazing, development (e.g., roads and ROWs), industrial

mineral extraction, and wildfire suppression.  These activities often result in increased 
soil erosion or compaction, which can lead to reduced soil fertility, water 
infiltration/retention, and vegetative cover.  These conditions may, in turn, cause 
secondary impacts such as sediment entering streams and lakes.  Changes in the type, 
extent, or intensity of these activities can reduce their impacts on soils. 
Livestock Grazing 
Under all of alternatives, soil protection is mandated by Central California Standards 
and Guidelines for Livestock Grazing, which specifies that soils should “exhibit 
functional biological and physical characteristics that are appropriate to soil type, climate, 
and land form.”  This means:  “Precipitation is able to enter the soil surface at appropriate 
rates; the soil is adequately protected against accelerated erosion; and the soil fertility is 
maintained at appropriate levels.”  If this standard is not being met, and livestock is 
determined to be the cause, BLM must take action to improve soil conditions.  This 
standard sets minimum criteria that apply to all of the alternatives.  Grazing can cause 
vegetation removal that allows rain to impact bare mineral soil and dislodge soil particles 
in localized areas.  Hooves also compact moist soil and loosen clods.  The amount of 
public land grazed would be greatest under Alternative C; therefore, adverse soil impacts 
would be likely be greater than for any other alternative.  However, because the intensity 
of grazing would not increase, these impacts would probably be minor and localized due 
to compliance with grazing standards and guidelines.  Alternative B would have the least 
impact because grazing leases would be reduced.  The Proposed RMP would be 
intermediate between Alternatives B and C. 
Transportation and Access (Motorized Vehicle/OHV Use Designations) 
Depending on scale, intensity, duration, and time of year, motorized use has the potential 
to impact soils.  Vehicles displace soil particles on dirt roads and cause compaction, 
rutting and gullies during wet conditions.  Gullies reroute water and often cause the roads 
to become wider as drivers try to avoid ruts, thus impacting soils outside the official road 
prism.  OHV use can have all of the same adverse effects on soils as well as damaging 
vegetation, which causes indirect impacts to soils.  Compaction and rutting are even more 
likely in off-road situations.  If high-impact use occurs near streams or other aquatic 
habitat, soil erosion could increase sedimentation and turbidity, therefore decreasing 
water quality and adversely affecting aquatic habitat.   
Alternative A would continue to allow all BLM lands to be open to OHV/motorized use 
(including off-road use), unless specifically closed.  All the other alternatives would limit 
OHV/motorized use to existing routes.  Under Alternative B and the Proposed RMP, a 
limited number of those existing routes would be designated as “open”; all other routes 
would be “closed.”  Under Alternative C, all existing open routes would remain open, but 
off-road use would not be permitted.  Under Alternative A, impacts to soils from 
motorized use would be greater than under any other alternative because vehicle use 
would be allowed over the largest area.

Wildland Fire Ecology and Management 
Periodic low-intensity wildfires are essential to the health of certain ecosystems.  Whole 
plant communities, such as chaparral, have adapted to periodic fires.  Although wildfires 
are a natural ecosystem process, high-intensity wildfires caused by extreme weather, 
artificially high fuel loading from decades of fire suppression, or human negligence can 
remove all vegetation, leading to accelerated erosion.  High-intensity fires can burn 
vegetation and organic matter down to bare mineral soil.  Extreme heating at the soil 
surface can produce hydrophobic soil that repels water, causing high surface runoff, and 
accelerated erosion.  In some ecosystems, invasive species have become dominant when 
the usual competitive advantage of native perennial species has been reduced or 
eliminated following intense wildfires.  Often, these are annual species with low ability to 
bind soils, which again fosters soil loss through erosion. 
Prescribed fire could result in short-term, localized, adverse impacts to soils through 
accelerated soil erosion.  However, long-term, beneficial impacts include reduced risk of 
severe wildfires, the recovery of a healthy native plant community that maintains soil 
stability, and reduced noxious weeds that often do little to bind soil particles. 
All alternatives would implement FFO’s Fire Management Plan.  Alternative A would 
use prescribed burns for fuel hazard reduction and wildfire suppression methods that have

The VRM class system was developed to guide the management of public lands,

resource management goals for that area.  The class can be higher or even lower than the

VRM class (I or II) reflects a strong desire to protect or enhance visual resources of the

power lines, or the building of large-scale roads.  Many such projects can have direct, 
adverse impacts on soils.

Cumulative Impacts 
Soil erosion could cumulatively impact site productivity, water quality, or sedimentation 
as soil particles become dislodged and transported by wind or water.  Natural soil erosion 
can be accelerated by road construction, residential development, vegetation removal, 
vehicle traffic on unpaved surfaces, grazing, and water gaining volume and velocity by 
collecting on impervious surfaces such as rooftops, paved roads, and parking lots.   
Management actions under the soil, water, and air quality programs are designed to 
improve soil resources.  Therefore, cumulative impacts occurring as a result of any of the 
soil management alternatives would be beneficial to the health and productivity of soil 
resources.  
Cumulative impacts from the proposed actions under other BLM programs would vary 
depending on the alternative selected.  Because many activities can affect soil erosion, 
including recreation, grazing, roads, and vegetation management, the cumulative impacts 
resulting from management actions under other BLM programs can vary greatly.  
BLM actions that produce erosion may adversely impact water resources on adjacent 
lands.  These impacts would be minimized through best management practices and 
project-specific planning.  Alternative B promotes low-intensity recreation and 
reclamation of redundant roads, and discourages soil-disturbing activities in sensitive 
areas, especially those that would have special designations.  This alternative would 
result in the fewest cumulative impacts because it would reduce erosion and sediment 
yield.  Alternative C and the Proposed RMP allow some soil-impacting activities and, 
therefore, would result in greater cumulative impacts.  Because Alternative C allows the 
most intensive level of soil disturbance, it has the greatest potential to result in adverse 
cumulative impacts on soil resources. 
Similarly, activities on lands adjacent to BLM lands have the potential to cause erosion.  
In particular, residential development, mining, and timber activities on adjacent lands 
have the potential to increase soil erosion through soil disturbance, exposure, and 
increased runoff.  These activities also may cause soil compaction from motorized 
vehicle travel and paving.

Wildland Fire Ecology and Management 
Periodic low-intensity wildfires are essential to the health of certain ecosystems.  Some 
vegetative species depend on fire to reproduce, while other whole plant communities, 
such as chaparral, have adapted to periodic fires.  Although wildfires are a natural 
ecosystem process, high-intensity wildfires caused by extreme weather, dense fuels, or 
human negligence can devastate vegetation, sometimes adversely impacting rare plant 
communities and special status plant species.  High-intensity fires can burn vegetation 
and organic matter down to bare earth.  This can damage soil, destroy roots, tubers, and 
rhizomes, at least temporarily replacing entire plant communities.  In some ecosystems, 
invasive species have become dominant when the usual competitive advantages of native 
perennial species have been reduced or eliminated following intense wildfires. 
Prescribed fire could benefit vegetation if used to reduce hazardous fuels, control or 
eliminate noxious weeds or invasive species, or increase plant community diversity.  
Prescribed fire can result in short-term, adverse impacts to vegetation-including direct 
mortality, plant injury, depletion of the seed bank, alteration of plant communities, weed 
increase, and accelerated soil erosion.  However, long-term, beneficial impacts include 
reduced risk of severe wildfires, reduction of noxious weeds or undesired non-native 
species, and increased species diversity of the plant community.  The prevention of 
severe wildfires is important because they can produce more intense versions of all of the 
potential adverse effects of a prescribed burn (listed above).

4.4.4 
Cumulative Impacts 
Because public lands managed by BLM are intermixed with private lands and other 
ownerships, beneficial cumulative impacts could result from the interaction of BLM 
vegetation management and the actions of private landowners and other agencies.  Under 
all the alternatives, BLM would work toward sustaining healthy vegetative communities, 
with an emphasis on protecting rare plant populations.  Generally, BLM would make a 
beneficial contribution to the conservation status of rare and declining plant communities.  
For many of these communities, however, the overall trend may be negative, as important 
habitat on private land becomes developed.  Public lands managed by other agencies, 
particularly by the USFS, provide habitat for some of the same vegetation that occurs on 
BLM lands.  These agencies generally benefit these vegetation types through habitat 
retention and improvement.  Because residential development, forestry, and mining on 
private lands remove vegetation and disturb soils, they would likely have an adverse 
impact on rare and declining plant communities, increasing the importance of habitat on 
public lands. 
Because vegetative communities cross property boundaries, habitat improvements on 
BLM lands may produce some positive benefits on adjacent lands.  This would be 
particularly evident with BLM’s proposed actions to control weeds.  Of course, without 
similar efforts on adjacent private lands, such efforts are not likely to produce long-term 
results.  Cooperation among landowners is a key to controlling weeds.  Weed 
Management Areas, Resource Conservation Districts, and CDF fuels projects all present 
opportunities for worthwhile vegetation treatments that span ownership boundaries.

4.6.1 
Introduction 
Refer to Section 2.6 for the proposed special status species management actions under 
each alternative, and refer to Section 3.6 for a description of existing special status

For ease of reference, the Chapter 2 management goals for special status species are: 
• Ensure all management activities and BLM authorizations on public lands are 
consistent with the conservation needs for special status species; and  
• Manage special status species habitat to assist in the recovery of listed species. 
Special status species include those plant and animal species:  federally listed as 
threatened, endangered, proposed, or candidates; listed by the state of California as 
threatened, endangered, or rare; or designated by BLM as sensitive.  The list of BLM 
sensitive plant species corresponds closely to the list of California Native Plant Society 
List 1B species which are “Plants rare, threatened or endangered in California and 
elsewhere.”  BLM sensitive species are managed in a manner to prevent the need for 
federal listing.  The restricted distributions, specialized habitat requirements, and 
population pressures (human and natural) facing special status species contribute to a 
high potential for extinction; thus, their populations are of conservation interest.   
The term “rare” is not an official BLM category, but it is used throughout this document 
to mean species that are uncommon and worthy of special management attention but that 
do not fit into BLM’s definition of special status species.  Examples would include 
species that have only one or a few populations in the region but are more common 
elsewhere, newly discovered species whose extent are unknown, and genotypes whose 
taxonomic status are yet to be determined.  Many of these rare species may become 
special status species during the next 20 years.

Under Alternative A, few areas have been assigned a VRM class because the system is 
relatively new and was not in use during the last major plan amendment.  Visual

Wildland Fire Ecology and Management 
Periodic low-intensity wildfires are essential to the health of certain ecosystems.  Some 
plant species, including some special status plant species, depend on fire to reproduce,

while other whole plant communities, such as chaparral, have adapted to periodic fires.  
Although wildfires are a natural ecosystem process, high-intensity wildfires caused by 
extreme weather, dense fuels, or human negligence can impact special status plants and 
animals.  Special status wildlife species that are particularly vulnerable to habitat 
disturbance include the California spotted owl, limestone salamander, and California red 
legged frog.  High-intensity fires can burn vegetation and organic matter down to bare 
mineral soil.  This can destroy roots, tubers, and rhizomes, at least temporarily replacing 
entire plant communities.  In some ecosystems, invasive species have become dominant 
when the usual competitive advantage of native perennial species has been reduced or 
eliminated following intense wildfires. 
Prescribed fire generally benefits special status plants and animals if the prescription is 
chosen to control or eliminate noxious weeds or undesired non-native species, foster the 
propagation of a special status plants that evolved under fire, or improve the habitat of a 
special status animal.   
Prescribed fire could result in short-term, adverse impacts to special status species, 
including mortality, injury, seed bank depletion, wildlife relocation, reduced prey, 
increased exposure to predation, temporary loss of food or shelter, and accelerated soil 
erosion.  However, long-term, beneficial impacts include reduced risk of severe wildfires, 
reduced noxious weeds or undesired non-native species, and increased propagation of 
some special status plant species.  Reducing the likelihood of severe wildfire is important 
because the potential adverse impacts of a prescribed fire or even more likely to occur in 
the event of a severe wildfire.  
All alternatives would implement BLM’s FMP.  In addition, Alternative A would use 
prescribed burns for fuel hazard reduction and would employ wildfire suppression 
methods that have the least impact on resource values in specified modified suppression 
zones.  For instance, when CDF fights a wildfire in the Red Hills or Limestone 
Salamander ACECs under the modified suppression plan for these areas, wide dozer lines 
that clear all vegetation down to mineral soil would be less likely to be used than they 
would be in other areas. 
Modified suppression plans would continue to be used under all of the alternatives.  
However, the alternatives with more special designations, such as Alternative B and the 
Proposed RMP, would allow more acres to be subject to modified suppression plans.  
Generally under modified suppression plans, fires that do not threaten lives or property 
are fought less aggressively to avoid or lessen long-term environmental impacts.  Of 
course, if lives or property are at risk, fire fighters will use every tool at their disposal to 
control the fire.  Under Alternative B and the Proposed RMP, potential short-term 
adverse impacts to special status species from modified suppression plans covering 
additional areas would include larger fires and more widespread alteration of habitat.  
Long-term impacts of increased, modified suppression plans would be a closer 
approximation of natural fire cycles, a more natural mosaic of different aged stands of 
vegetation, and reduced long-term modification of habitat due to the alteration of soils 
that accompanies heavy equipment use during standard fire suppression.  Dozer 
operations can be the most destructive aspects of wildfires for special status species.

4.6.4 
Cumulative Impacts 
Because public lands managed by BLM are intermixed with private lands and other 
ownerships, beneficial cumulative impacts could result from the interaction of BLM 
vegetation management and the actions of private landowners and other agencies.  Under 
all the alternatives, BLM would work toward conserving healthy ecosystems, with an 
emphasis on special status plants and animals and their habitats.  Generally, BLM would 
make a beneficial contribution to the conservation status of rare and special status plants 
and animals.  For many of these species, the overall conservation trend may be negative 
as important habitat on private land becomes developed.  Public lands managed by other 
agencies, including the USFS, NPS, and CDPR, provide habitat for some of the same 
special status species that occur on BLM land.  These agencies generally benefit these 
species through habitat retention, improvement, and other work.  Residential 
development, forestry, and mining on private lands would likely have an adverse impact 
on rare and special status species that occur in the planning area, thus increasing the 
importance of habitat on public lands. 
Since special status species and their habitats cross property boundaries, habitat 
improvements on BLM lands would likely benefit adjacent lands.  This would be 
particularly evident with BLM weed control.  Of course, without similar efforts on 
adjacent private lands, BLM actions are not likely to produce long-term, permanent 
results because invasive species would likely reinvade public lands.  Cooperation among 
landowners is key to controlling weeds.  Weed Management Areas, Resource 
Conservation Districts, and CDF fuels projects all present opportunities for weed control 
that spans ownership boundaries. 
Although Alternatives A and C could cause beneficial cumulative impacts on special 
status species, Alternative B and the Proposed RMP would make a greater beneficial 
contribution to special status species populations across ownership boundaries because 
these alternatives contain the most proactive special status species management actions.

Air Quality 
The air quality proposed actions laid out in Chapter 2 direct BLM to meet local, state, and 
federal air quality standards.  Without question, these standards are beneficial to air 
quality, people, and the environment, but they do sometimes cause minor to moderate 
adverse long-term impacts on fuels management.  The timing of prescribed burns is 
critical.  To be effective, the burns must occur within prescription (temperature, time of 
day, time of year, humidity, etc.) and with adequate numbers of firefighting resources 
present.  This can be an extremely small window in time:  perhaps a few weeks or even a 
few days.  Land managers must sometimes hold off from igniting prescribed burns 
because local officials predict air quality would be temporarily impacted by prescribed 
burning.  Agencies such as BLM have had to wait until the following year (window of 
opportunity) to implement prescribed burn projects.  
Vegetative Communities 
Under all of the alternatives, the vegetation proposed actions would improve existing 
conditions by controlling invasive species and by promoting healthy and diverse 
vegetation.  This would have long-term beneficial impacts on fire management in the 
planning area.  Excessive vegetation (dense brush, conifer crowding, etc.) and weed 
infestations are sure signs of unhealthy ecological conditions and are at risk of severe 
wildfire.  Vegetation proposed actions (fuel reduction, weed control, stand thinning, etc.) 
would reduce the severity of these conditions.  Alternative B and the Proposed RMP

because of their focus on habitat enhancement.

Transportation and Access 
The greatest threat to paleontological resources on BLM land has been theft and damage 
caused by off-road motorized use. 
Under Alternative A, motorized use would be allowed throughout the planning area 
unless otherwise designated as closed.  This extensive use, including off-road use, would 
likely have moderately adverse impacts on paleontological resources due to increased 
access and ground disturbance caused by off-road OHV use.  This alternative would 
afford the least protection to paleontological resources compared with the other 
alternatives. 
Alternatives B, C, and the Proposed RMP would limit motorized use in the planning area.  
These alternatives would limit access to paleontological resources, thereby resulting in 
fewer adverse impacts than under Alternative A.  Alternative C would limit motorized 
use to existing routes that have not already been closed by a previous BLM action.  This 
alternative would have a beneficial impact on paleontological resources, but it would be 
less than Alternative B and the Proposed RMP, which would limit motorized use to 
designated routes.  The designated routes scenario would prohibit access to 
paleontological resources, which would provide the greatest protection from looting or 
vehicle damage of all the alternatives.  
4.9.4 
Cumulative Impacts 
Adverse impacts on paleontological resources on non-BLM lands in the planning area 
may occur from residential development on private lands and from mining and timber 
activities.  Alternative A could result in cumulative impacts because paleontological 
resources on BLM land would not be protected from motorized use.

4.10.2 Impacts of VRM Proposed Actions on Visual Resources 
Under Alternative A, BLM would continue to manage visual resources according to 
federal laws, regulations, policies and existing VRM classifications.  Under Alternative 
A, areas that have not previously received VRM classes would be assessed on a case-by-
case basis using existing VRM inventory data.  Though outstanding visual resources 
managed by BLM would continue to receive consideration and protection under 
Alternative A, the impacts of this alternative could be moderately adverse and long term.  
A case-by-case strategy, as proposed under this alternative, discourages the management 
of visual resources on a viewshed scale.  BLM manages considerable amounts of public 
land that have not been assigned a VRM class.  These areas include the North Fork/Main 
Stem Mokelumne River canyon, the Lake Don Pedro/Highway 49 viewshed, and the 
Lake Mclure/Highway 49 viewshed.  The management of visual resources in these areas 
is becoming increasingly important to the public (due to urban encroachment) and would 
be improved by the assignment of VRM classes, which encourages a more even, 
consistent approach to dealing with visual resource issues.    
Alternative B proposes a management scenario that would be the most beneficial to 
visual resources compared to the other alternatives.  Under Alternative B, BLM would 
manage all land as either Class I or Class II, the most protective VRM classes.  Areas 
such as the North Fork Mokelumne, Middle Fork Mokelumne, Turnback Creek, and 
Merced River WSA would be managed as Class I.  Activities that might degrade these 
visual resources (i.e., ROW/road construction, large-scale mining, timber sales, etc.) 
would not be authorized or would be redesigned to minimize visual impacts.  
Under Alternative C, most BLM land in the planning area, 200,000 acres, would receive 
Class III status.  A small amount of land, approximately 30,000 acres, would be managed 
as Class I or II, including WSR corridors and areas within community based plans.  
Outstanding visual resources would be protected under this management scenario; 
however, many high-quality but less prominent visual resources would not benefit from 
protection afforded by a Class II status as they would under Alternative B.  BLM might 
be more likely under Alternative C to authorize activities in these areas that are beneficial 
to recreation, economic development, and other public interests but that might degrade 
visual resources.  The impacts of Alternative C on visual resources would probably be 
adverse but minor. 
The Proposed RMP would balance protection of visual resources with meeting public 
demands to use BLM land in ways that might degrade visual resources.  These uses could 
include high-voltage transmission line construction, large-scale mining, timber sales, etc.  
A wide variety of viewsheds, landscape, and specific visual resources would receive

Resources 
Lands and Realty (Land Ownership Adjustment) 
All of the alternatives could be viewed as having a long-term beneficial impact on visual 
resources because under each management scenario, BLM would strive to consolidate 
land in areas with outstanding visual resources or maintain areas (viewsheds) with 
considerable amounts of BLM land.  
Under Alternative A, BLM would focus on providing access to public lands, 
consolidating BLM ownership in river corridors, and acquiring additional special status 
habitat.  This would have long-term beneficial impacts on visual resources. 
Under Alternative B, the emphasis would be on acquiring riparian habitat, blue oak 
woodland, Central Valley wetlands, vernal pools, and significant cultural resources.  An 
important goal under Alternative B would be to increase ACEC acreage, including the 
Red Hills ACEC and Pine Hill Preserve, both of which are important viewsheds.  The 
visual impacts of Alternative B, therefore, would be long term and beneficial.   
Alternative C would consolidate BLM ownership in SRMAs and WSR corridors.  The 
proposed South Yuba River, North Fork American River, and Merced River SRMAs are 
also partly in WSR corridors known for their outstanding visual resources.  BLM would 
attempt to consolidate its ownership in these areas to protect and enhance visual 
resources.  The impacts would be long term and beneficial. 
The Proposed RMP is similar to Alternative A.  It would direct BLM to consolidate land 
ownership in areas with either outstanding resources, high recreational values, or both.  
Under this alternative, BLM would try to acquire and protect a wide range of important 
visual resources (Sierra Nevada river canyons, Central Valley wetlands, the Red Hills) in 
the planning area.

Other BLM Programs

4.10.4 Cumulative Impacts 
Many federal and state controlled public lands abut or are near BLM lands.  These 
agencies utilize the VRM system for classifying their holdings and are probably 
managing visual resources consistent with BLM.  Private property in the planning area is 
not subject to VRM requirements and policies, and private landowners are not required to 
follow VRM guidelines except in certain cases, when they require a federal or state 
permit.  Private lands can be developed or utilized for agricultural, industrial, residential, 
or commercial uses without attention to overall visual resource issues.  Cumulative 
impacts to visual resources could occur as development pressure increases in the planning 
area.  Observers on BLM land will be more likely to see an altered landscape as private 
land development continues.  This is especially true for smaller BLM parcels that abut 
growing urban areas.  Because Alternative B and the Proposed RMP would allow the 
least degradation of visual resources, they also have the least potential for cumulative 
impacts.  Potential impacts from Alternative C, which has less stringent visual resource 
objectives, would be offset by careful project planning, public review, best management 
practices, and mitigation measures.  BLM’s goal of consolidating land in key river 
viewsheds would go a long way to avoiding cumulative impacts.

Caves 
4.11.1 Introduction 
Refer to Section 2.11 for the proposed caves management actions under each alternative, 
and refer to Section 3.11 for a description of existing cave conditions in the planning 
area.   
For ease of reference, the management goal for caves is restated below:  
• Manage caves to protect and maintain significant cave resources in the 
planning area. 
4.11.2 Impacts of the Caves Program’s Proposed Actions on Caves 
There are no proposed actions specific to cave resources under Alternative A. 
Accordingly, a lack of management direction could result in adverse impacts on cave 
resources because BLM would not likely take proactive steps to reduce the chance for 
cave disturbance or take other necessary management actions.    
Alternatives B, C, and the Proposed RMP include proposed actions specific to the Crystal 
Palace Cave.  This cave is perhaps the most extensive, well-known, and important cave 
resource in the planning area.  
Under Alternatives B, C, and the Proposed RMP, BLM would complete a geospatial 
survey of Crystal Palace Cave to determine its location with respect to BLM- and 
USFS-managed lands.  This cave resource would benefit from this survey because cave 
management is dependent on accurate locational information.   
Under Alternative B, BLM would conduct a study to determine whether Crystal Palace 
Cave is significant according to federal regulations.  BLM would also develop a plan to 
manage the cave.  Both proposed actions would have a long-term beneficial impact on 
the cave.  Overall, Alternative B would likely have the greatest beneficial impact on cave 
resources because it would require BLM to take the most proactive steps to learn about 
and manage the Crystal Place Cave.    
4.11.3 Impacts of Other BLM Programs’ Proposed Actions on Caves  
The limestone caves that occur on BLM land in the planning area are fragile and can be 
impacted by a variety of activities.  Perhaps the most damaging activity is casual use by 
people who vandalize the caves by carving their names in the wall or removing cave 
features such as stalagmites.  Fragile cave-dwelling wildlife such as rare bats and other 
species could be disturbed.  Increased access generally causes increased damage to caves.  
Transportation and access are key to this analysis.

Transportation and Access 
Under Alternative A, all BLM land not previously closed would be open to motorized 
use, including cross-country use.  Such activities could adversely impact cave resources 
because of easy access to caves.  Many caves on BLM land are already being used by the 
public on a regular basis.  However, use of motorized vehicles in close proximity to cave 
entrances may disrupt sensitive flora and fauna that inhabit caves.  Alternative A might 
result in minor adverse impacts on caves. 
Under Alternative C, OHV use would be limited to existing routes that have not 
previously been closed by BLM.  This is far better than Alternative A in terms of cave 
protection, but there could be adverse impacts on caves as a result of OHV access. 
Alternative B and the Proposed RMP would be the most aggressive in limiting access to 
fragile caves.  These alternatives would restrict motorized vehicle/OHV use to designated 
roads.  They also would decrease unauthorized OHV route development, thereby 
reducing access to caves in the planning area.  Alternative B and the Proposed RMP 
would result in the greatest beneficial impacts on cave resources of all the alternatives 
considered.  
Special Status Species (Conservation Strategies)  
The conservation strategies (Appendix B) developed with the USFWS promote the 
preservation and protection of bats and bat habitat, which includes some caves.  These 
conservation strategies would be adopted under Alternative B and the Proposed RMP.  
Therefore, the implementation of these alternatives would likely have a beneficial impact 
on cave resources.  
Under Alternatives A and C, practices to protect bat habitat are not specified; therefore, 
this alternative has the possibility to result in more adverse impacts than the other 
alternatives because it would not provide as much active protection of caves/cave-
dwelling bats on BLM land. 
4.11.4 Cumulative Impacts 
Adverse cumulative impacts to cave resources could occur under Alternatives A and C 
because the relative lack of access restrictions associated with these alternatives might 
enable users of other federal, state, or private lands to access caves located on BLM-
managed lands.  In addition, potential closure to pubic access of caves on other lands may 
relocate more cave enthusiasts to cave resources in the Sierra Planning Area, which could 
result in increased disruption to physical cave elements and wildlife that utilize caves as 
habitat.

Forestry 
4.12.1 Introduction 
Refer to Section 2.12 for the proposed forestry and timber management actions under 
each alternative, and refer to Section 3.12 for a description of the forestry resources in the 
planning area.  Forestry is also addressed in Table ES-1 on page 4 of the Executive 
Summary. 
For ease of plan reference, the management goal from Chapter 2 is reiterated here: 
• Manage all forests and woodlands under the principles of multiple use, 
sustained yield, and protection of the environment in accordance with federal 
laws, regulations, and policies.  
4.12.2 Impacts of the Forestry Program’s Proposed Actions on Forestry  
All four alternatives would incorporate community based planning, which involves active 
participation by the public.  To date, this planning process has played a major role in 
forest management in the planning area. 
Timber management for all BLM forestlands would allow for multiple use, sustained 
yield, and environmental protection.  Management would focus on forest ecological 
conditioning, improving forest health, increasing vigor and resistance to insect or disease 
epidemics, reducing catastrophic wildfire hazard, and developing old growth attributes 
(e.g., multi-layered canopies, large snags, downed logs, and large diameter trees).  The 
natural processes of growth and decay would be encouraged to allow the reestablishment 
of old growth forest conditions, stand health, and stand resiliency. 
Forest products would include timber and fuelwood harvesting.  Timber harvesting would 
include salvage logging of diseased, damaged, or hazardous trees as well as thinning of 
green trees to improve forest health and reduce hazardous fuels.  
Alternative A would manage forests for sustained yield consistent with environmental 
quality and relevant community based plans.  Prescribed fire and mechanical treatments 
would improve timber production and reduce the risk of catastrophic wildfire.  Improving 
forest health would be an important component of management.  These actions would 
have long-term benefits on the forestry program and would create additional 
opportunities for companies to buy and harvest BLM timber.  
Alternative B would manage for the maintenance and development of old growth 
coniferous forests and enhanced forest health.  This alternative would allow salvage 
timber sales but would be mainly oriented toward improving forest health and creating 
old growth stands.  There would be a long-term beneficial impact to old growth habitat 
and forest health under this alternative.  There would be fewer opportunities for 
companies to buy and harvest timber than in the other alternatives.

Alternative C would manage forests more intensively and provide more timber volume 
than the other alternatives.  Alternative C would increase tree harvesting over the next  
20 years and increase plantation maintenance.  Adverse impacts from tree harvesting 
would be minimal to moderate, and the time of recovery would depend on harvest rates, 
soil disturbance, and rehabilitation.  This alternative would provide the greatest 
opportunity for companies to buy and harvest BLM timber.   
The Proposed RMP would manage for forest health and timber production, depending on 
the area and the outcome of community based plans.  In some areas, communities may 
want to see local forestland managed in a way that creates old growth conditions.  In 
other areas, community based planning may reflect a desire for increased timber 
production.  The Proposed RMP provides the best long-term, sustainable forest 
production compared to the other alternatives.  Fuels reduction and plantation 
maintenance would occur where needed.  The impacts of the Proposed RMP are nearly 
the same as under Alternative A.  Compared to Alternative B there would be more 
opportunities for timber companies, but the opportunities would probably not be as 
numerous as under Alternative C.    
Overall, Alternative B and the Proposed RMP would all provide similar protection and

consumptive uses while refining woodland inventories.  Rehabilitation of disturbed areas 
would occur, providing long-term benefits to the resource.  These alternatives would 
require compliance with the Timber Harvest Criteria (Appendix D).  
4.12.3 Impacts of Other BLM Programs’ Proposed Actions on Forestry 
Special Designations (ACECs and Wild and Scenic Rivers) 
On special designation lands (e.g., ACECs and wild and scenic rivers), forest 
management would be oriented towards environmental protection and salvage of 
damaged timber rather than commodity production.  
Under Alternative A, no new special designations are proposed, although the existing 
WSA, WSRs, and ACECs would continue to be managed as they have been, placing the 
same level of constraints on timber harvest opportunities. 
Under Alternative B, designation of eight new ACECs, three ACEC additions, and seven 
wild and scenic rivers would increase protection of special status species, paleontological 
resources, and outstanding river corridors.  These new designations might result in the 
unavailability of these areas to green timber sales which could be a moderately adverse 
impact to timber harvesting.  The overall effect on total harvest volume, however, would 
be slight; these special designation lands are not well stocked with timber.  The net result 
would be a negligible adverse impact to the timber program. 
Only one new special designation would be proposed under Alternative C.  This would 
leave a larger amount of BLM land open to green timber sales, which would constitute a

long-term, beneficial impact to the timber program; the volume harvested would 
potentially be greater than in Alternative B.  
The Proposed RMP proposes seven new ACECs, three ACEC additions, and two WSRs.  
These designations would probably increase protection for vegetation, resulting in the

Wildland Fire Ecology and Management  
BLM’s fire program is expected to benefit the forestry program.  The plan calls for the 
removal of hazardous fuels across the planning area.  This would benefit forested areas 
where natural fire cycles have been altered.  Historical fire suppression has caused the 
fuel hazard to increase.  In this case, wildfires burn hotter, spread more quickly, and 
consume more plant material than historical fires occurring under conditions of lower 
fuel loading.  Restoring and maintaining fire-adapted forests would decrease the effects 
from wildfire to forest communities and improve their resilience and sustainability. 
Alternative A would use prescribed fire and other vegetation treatments to reduce fuel 
hazards (with a goal to limit 90% of all wildfires to less than 10 acres).  Fire suppression 
techniques would be modified to reduce impacts in the ‘Inimim Forest, Round Mountain, 
all WSR corridors, the Merced River WSA, Pine Hill Preserve, and in all ACECs.  Full 
fire suppression would occur in other areas, while hazardous fuels would be reduced in 
the WUI and communities-at-risk.  Fuel reduction projects specified in community based 
plans would be prioritized.  These actions would constitute a moderate beneficial impact 
to the forestry and timber management program through reduced fuel loadings and 
improved forest health and resiliency. 
Fire management actions under Alternatives B, C, and the Proposed RMP would not 
change appreciably from Alternative A.  Under Alternative B, fuels reduction projects 
that benefit significant biological and cultural resources would be prioritized.  Under 
Alternative C, priority would be given to fuel reduction projects for communities at risk.  
The Proposed RMP would prioritize fuels reduction projects to benefit both communities 
at risk and significant natural and cultural resources.  Fire management actions under 
Alternatives B, C, and the Proposed RMP would have negligible impacts on the forestry 
management program.

standard for visual resource management, and could affect timber sales and other forestry 
program actions if disturbance were to exceed the thresholds specified for the visual

4.13.2 Impacts of the Livestock Grazing Program’s Proposed Actions on 
Livestock Grazing  
All alternatives would continue to make progress toward improved rangeland health 
through continued compliance with the Central California Standards and Guidelines for 
Livestock Grazing.  Grazing activity would be altered in leases not meeting these 
standards and guidelines.  Under Alternatives B, C, and the Proposed RMP, BLM would 
suspend grazing activities where monitoring indicates adverse impacts on special status 
species are occurring.  Because grazing and special status species conflicts are rare in the 
planning area, impacts on grazing due to special status species conflicts would be 
negligible and further reduced if grazing were removed from the Red Hills ACEC. 
Under Alternative A, grazing would be managed to provide 700 pounds of residual mulch 
per acre and to increase forage production.  Alternative A would benefit grazing 
opportunities.  
Some leases are small and not easily grazed due to steep topography, unsuitable or sparse 
vegetation, and poor administrative access.  Reducing leases over time would benefit 
BLM management by simplifying administration.  Alternative B emphasizes 
environmental protection.  Under this alternative, grazing would be reduced by 
eventually phasing out leases that do not meet the threshold of 100 AUMs.  Leases less 
than 100 AUMs would be considered unmanageable and would be relinquished or 
cancelled upon renewal.  Reductions in grazing allocations would reduce BLM’s 
administrative cost, but would have a long-term, adverse impact on grazing opportunities.

4.14.4 Cumulative Impacts 
The proposed actions would have a low potential to cause adverse cumulative impacts.  
The most economically important mineral resources managed by BLM would remain 
available for development at virtually the same levels under all of the alternatives.  These 
include sand and gravel deposits in the Yuba Goldfields, high-potential oil and gas areas 
in the Central Valley, and locatable gold and other solid minerals in the Sierra Nevada 
foothills.  Yuba Goldfields’ sand and gravel is clearly the most economically important 
mineral resource in the planning area.  Under all of the alternatives, this resource would 
be available for extraction.  
Some BLM land would be proposed for withdrawal from mineral development.  The 
proposed withdrawals under Alternative B and the Proposed RMP are most notable.  This 
would reduce opportunities for locatable mineral development.  Overall, the mineral 
potential of the lands proposed for withdrawal is not high.  
Minerals development impacts would likely be minor and would contribute little to the 
overall impacts (adverse and beneficial) caused by mining on non-BLM land in the 
planning area.  Since BLM lands provide a relatively small percentage of available 
minerals extraction area in the Western Sierra, cumulative impacts from BLM actions are 
negligible to the overall mineral extraction industry.  Mitigation measures placed on 
drilling permits would reduce the potential for cumulative impacts, such as contamination 
of water resources or harm to wildlife in national wildlife refuges.  The extraction of sand 
and gravel from the Yuba Goldfields would probably result in economic benefits for the 
local community, with the creation of jobs.

4.15.4 Cumulative Impacts 
There are two possible adverse cumulative impacts.  First, BLM’s effort to accommodate 
increased recreation demands may lead to additional recreation demands, which may far 
exceed those currently anticipated.  There are numerous recreational opportunities in the 
planning area.  Outstanding opportunities exist on public lands managed by the CDRC, 
USBR, USFS, and NPS.  Among these public land managers, BLM has been in a unique 
position to provide recreational opportunities very near areas experiencing rapid 
population growth.  BLM recreation areas such as the Cronan Ranch on the South Fork 
American River are within a short driving distance of metropolitan Sacramento and other 
regional urban areas.   
The construction of additional proposed parking areas, bathrooms, trails, etc., in popular 
BLM recreation areas may spur additional demand as people find out about these areas 
and return with their friends and family.  BLM could become the victim of its own 
success by creating a wealth of recreational opportunities on public lands that are easily 
accessible to a growing population.  This scenario is speculative, and it is difficult to say 
which alternative would be best for alleviating the potential for these kinds of adverse 
cumulative impacts.  Under Alternative B, BLM would emphasize environmental 
protection rather than recreation.  Under this alternative, BLM may be able to head off 
the problem of BLM lands becoming so popular that they become overrun, diminishing 
the experience for all user groups.  This may also be possible under the Proposed RMP, 
but to a lesser extent.  The recreation and access emphasis of Alternative C may better 
accommodate increased public demands over time than the other alternatives.

The second possible impact concerns the increasing popularity of OHV recreation.  It 
usually requires large areas and route networks to prevent conflicts between riders and to 
avoid impacts to adjacent private property.  Driving cross-country off existing routes is 
popular with many OHV users, but it can take its toll on the environment.  Off-road use 
can destroy vegetation, damage cultural resources, disturb wildlife, and cause erosion, 
compaction, and sedimentation.  BLM’s land ownership pattern can be incompatible with 
OHV use.  BLM manages relatively small tracts of public lands, which are often brushy 
and have steep terrain, providing few OHV opportunities.  As a result, BLM proposes to 
limit OHV use to existing routes (under Alternative C) or to designated routes (under 
Alternative B and the Proposed RMP).   
Restricting motorized use as proposed under Alternatives B, C, and the Proposed RMP, 
could displace motorized use to the jurisdiction of other regional land managers, such as 
California State Parks or the USFS, which could, in turn, outstrip their capacity to 
accommodate the additional use.  This would be especially true for land managers not 
prepared for additional visitors.  There are currently few OHV parks in the planning area.  
The USFS provides routes and other facilities for OHV users, but substantial sections of 
national forests have been closed or limited to OHV use.  Overcrowding and overuse 
could lead to additional conflicts among user groups.  However, this is unlikely to occur 
because currently, BLM land receives little OHV use.  OHV use is increasing, but the 
expected cumulative impact of limiting this use to existing or designated routes on BLM

in the region.  Scattered BLM parcels with poor access provide few opportunities for this 
use.

4.16.2 Impacts of the Transportation and Access Proposed Actions on 
Transportation and Access  
Under Alternative A, cross-country motorized use would be allowed.  With increasing 
OHV use throughout the planning area, this could lead to an unsafe transportation system 
that would not be feasible for BLM to manage.  As the route system continued to 
develop, access would become less straightforward to the public.  Motorists could get lost 
or stuck on newly developed routes.  Given the scattered nature of BLM lands, impacts to 
adjacent private property (dust, noise, trespass, etc.) would be unavoidable because 
virtually all of the routes BLM manages are route segments that traverse public and 
private land.  Working with private landowners to resolve trespass problems could place 
a tremendous management burden on BLM.  
Alternative C has many of the same problems that Alternative A has, except that cross-
country travel would not be permitted under Alternative C.  Many existing routes have 
been created without BLM authorization or have become unsafe to drive, even for dirt 
bikes.  Under Alternative C, the system would remain unsafe and difficult for BLM to 
manage.  Adverse impacts to private property would still occur on a wide scale due to 
trespass while accessing BLM roads.  
Alternative B and the Proposed RMP narrow BLM’s transportation system down to key 
designated routes that ensure the public would have straightforward, safe access to many 
BLM lands, including trailheads, campgrounds, boat launches, and other developed 
recreation areas.  This system of designated routes would facilitate access to large blocks 
of public lands, prevent impacts (trespass, noise, etc.) to private landowners, and 
maintain the regional transportation network.  Also, the system could be feasibly 
managed by BLM and would reduce human-caused wildfire ignitions because fewer 
routes would be open to OHVs that could throw sparks into dry vegetation.  These 
alternatives would have fewer adverse impacts on cultural resources than Alternative A, 
which permits cross-country travel.  
OHV users who want to ride cross-country would be constrained by Alternatives B, C, 
and the Proposed RMP.  In this respect, these alternatives could be seen as having 
adverse impacts on public land access.

4.17.1 Introduction 
Refer to Section 2.17 for the proposed lands and realty management actions under each 
alternative, and refer to Section 3.17 for a description of existing lands and realty actions 
in the planning area.  Lands and realty are also addressed in Table ES-1 on page 6 of the 
Executive Summary.  This section describes the impacts on the lands and realty program 
(including land ownership adjustment) and on opportunities for the public and local 
governments to receive various authorizations (ROWs, R&PP Act leases, etc.).  For ease 
of reference, the management goal for lands and realty is restated below:   
• Develop a public land pattern which enhances resource values and uses. 
4.17.2 Impacts of the Lands and Realty Proposed Actions on the Lands 
and Realty Program 
Land Ownership Adjustment 
Under Alternative A, BLM would acquire and dispose of lands on a case-by-case basis.  
Some improved efficiencies in the management of public lands would be realized through 
consolidation of public lands, including reduced conflicts with other landowners and 
increased management efficiency.  Although this alternative would provide some 
direction for the acquisition and disposal of land, more specific direction is needed.  To 
the extent that the existing situation is deficient in criteria for land acquisition, this could 
be considered an adverse impact on the lands and realty program.   
Under Alternatives B, C, and the Proposed RMP, BLM would retain public lands in 
ACECs, SRMAs, the WSA, lands with critical watershed values adjacent to major water 
bodies, and WSR corridors.  BLM would also retain lands with significant cultural and 
biological resources, including federally listed species and cultural resources eligible for 
inclusion on the National Register of Historic Places.  These alternatives would benefit 
land ownership patterns by:  enhancing the management of these protected areas; 
reducing administrative costs to BLM with the disposal of unmanageable and 
uneconomic parcels with low resource value; and providing more effective land 
management.  All of the alternatives, to different degrees, would have a beneficial effect 
on BLM’s lands and realty program (see specific alternatives below).  The management 
actions would lead to more efficient management of the public lands and would protect 
important biological, cultural, and recreational resources. 
Under Alternative B, land ownership adjustment would focus on preserving and 
protecting the environment.  BLM would retain public lands with BLM sensitive species 
and state listed species (in addition to the lands and resources stated under Common to 
Alternatives B, C, and the Proposed RMP).  Additional cultural resources may be 
retained.  Scattered tracts with low resource values would be targeted for disposal.  This 
strategy would consolidate lands with important resource values in public ownership,

thus benefiting the lands and realty program by opening up various opportunities for land 
exchanges, sales, etc., involving high-quality environmental resources. 
Under Alternative C, land ownership adjustment would focus on obtaining high-quality 
recreation land.  This would benefit the lands and realty program by opening up various 
opportunities for land exchanges, sales, etc., involving high-quality recreation resources. 
The Proposed RMP is a compromise between Alternatives B and C.  Land acquisitions to 
expand ACECs, SRMAs, and WSR corridors would be emphasized.  This alternative 
would best address the goals of the lands and realty program by giving it the most 
flexibility in pursuing various opportunities.  This alternative would, therefore, have the 
greatest beneficial impact. 
Land Use Authorizations 
There are no impacts identified under Alternative A.  The preservation and protection 
emphasis of Alternative B could potentially reduce opportunities for the public to receive 
land use authorizations through BLM’s lands and realty program.  Land use 
authorizations that potentially damage sensitive environmental resources would be 
denied.  Alternative C and the Proposed RMP, which would require BLM to make 
authorizations on a case-by-case basis, responds more effectively to current and future 
demand for land use authorizations.    
Withdrawals 
Generally, the mineral withdrawals proposed under the four alternatives would benefit 
natural and cultural resource programs, but would pose an adverse impact on 
opportunities for the development of locatable mineral resources.  Valid, existing rights 
would be protected under all alternatives.  The impact would be greatest under 
Alternative B and the Proposed RMP, which propose the greatest number of withdrawals.   
4.17.3 Impacts of Other BLM Programs’ Proposed Actions on the Lands 
and Realty Program 
Special Status Species 
To promote the preservation and recovery of special status species, BLM would be 
encouraged to acquire land with potential habitat for special status plant and animal 
species to some extent under all alternatives.  This would benefit special status species.  
Designation of areas for protection of special status species could limit some ROW 
authorizations.  See Section 4.6, Special Status Species, for information on specific areas 
that would be affected under each alternative. 
Conservation strategies proposed under Alternative B and the Proposed RMP could affect 
the lands and realty program by limiting the location of utility facilities or other 
authorized land uses.  The strategies could also play a part in determining which lands 
would be acquired or whether some land exchanges could occur.

Special Designations 
BLM may limit opportunities for various kinds of land use authorizations to protect 
special designation values.  Alternative B would have the most special designations and 
would, therefore, present the greatest impact on the lands and realty program.  Alternative 
C would have the fewest special designations and would cause the least impact on land 
use authorizations.  The impacts of the Proposed RMP would fall somewhere between 
Alternatives B and C.    
Visual Resources 
The restrictions that some areas would be placed under to protect visual quality could 
affect the lands and realty program.  For example, BLM might not approve transmission 
lines, communication sites, or other structures in VRM Class I or II areas.  Impacts on the 
lands and realty program would be greatest under Alternative B, which would create the 
greatest amount of Class I and II areas.  Lesser impacts to the lands and realty program 
would occur under Alternative C and the Proposed RMP. 
4.17.4 Cumulative Impacts 
The cumulative impact of the lands and realty program would likely be beneficial.  The 
consolidation of public land with recreational and environmental resources, as proposed 
in all of the alternatives to one degree or another, would benefit communities, tourists, 
and others who enjoy the central Sierra Nevada foothills.  This area is experiencing rapid 
growth, and there is great demand for open space, places to recreate, and environmental 
protection.  BLM’s management strategy addresses this demand and helps compensate 
for a loss of open space due to development.      
As discussed in more detail in the section on social and economic impacts (4.20), 
retention of BLM lands would likely increase the value of land in many residential areas.  
Other federal lands in the planning area have caused similar increases in community real 
estate values and demands. 
Growing residential and commercial development may lead to an increase in applications 
to BLM for ROWs for access roads, utility lines, and communication facilities.  The 
alternatives primarily provide for considering how best to meet these needs on a case-by-
case basis.

Hazardous Materials and Abandoned Mine Lands 
4.18.1 Introduction 
Refer to Section 2.18 for the proposed hazardous materials and abandoned mine lands 
management actions, and refer to Section 3.18 for a description of the existing conditions 
relating to hazardous materials and abandoned mine lands in the planning area.  For ease 
of reference, the management goal for hazardous materials and abandoned mine lands is 
restated below: 
• Minimize hazardous conditions on BLM lands to reduce risks to the public 
and to ensure environmental health and safety. 
4.18.2 Impacts of the Program’s Proposed Actions on Hazardous 
Materials and Abandoned Mine Lands 
Management actions specified in Section 2.18 are common to all alternatives.  
Accordingly, impacts would be beneficial under all alternatives because the management 
actions represent measures to prevent releases of hazardous materials, remediate known 
sites contaminated with hazardous materials, and protect the public from physical hazards 
on abandoned mine lands.  In addition, BLM is required by federal, state, and local 
regulations to collect, store, and dispose of hazardous materials and wastes appropriately.   
These beneficial impacts are additionally ensured by implementing the recommendations 
from the past and future Compliance Assessment Safety, Health, and Environment 
(CASHE) audits.  Such recommendations may include correcting deficiencies in storing 
hazardous materials, disposal practices for hazardous wastes, and other possible findings 
identified in the CASHE audits.   
4.18.3 Impacts of Other BLM Programs’ Proposed Actions on Hazardous 
Materials and Abandoned Mine Lands 
Water Resources 
Where water resources are contaminated by discharge of mine-related wastes, Clean 
Water Act enforcement actions would have long-term beneficial impacts.  Remediation 
of mercury waste sites can control the off-site migration into adjacent surface waters, 
resulting in enhanced water quality. 
Cultural Resources 
Cultural resources significant for their historic values are sometimes affected by 
AML-hazmat concerns.  Workings, structures, and buildings related to historic mining 
can have both historic significance and contaminant issues.  Presence of toxic waste can 
constrain management for historic values, and, conversely, presence of historic values 
can complicate remediation of hazmat sites.  An optimal management strategy often 
involves accommodation and compromise.  In some cases where BLM proposes to

develop an interpretive historic site, and contaminated mine waste must be cleaned up to 
insure public safety, the hazmat remediation can benefit the cultural and AML programs. 
Special Status Species (Conservation Strategies) 
Alternative B and the Proposed RMP include conservation strategies for fish and wildlife 
(Appendix B) that protect bat habitat, which often occurs in abandoned mine tunnels, 
shafts, or mill buildings.  BLM’s ability to enhance public safety or reduce contaminants 
from these features could be complicated by the conservation strategies in the following 
ways: 
• It is not desirable to block mine tunnels/shafts in such a way as to prevent bat 
ingress and regress.  This can eliminate from consideration some simple and 
economical methods of closure.  However, “bat gates” at tunnel/shaft 
entrances may be successfully employed. 
• It may be desirable to keep abandoned mill structures intact if they are used by 
bats for roosting.  This is a potential resource protection/public safety conflict 
if building materials are sources of contaminants for the public or 
environment. 
Due to the conservations strategies, some AML remediation projects would be redesigned 
or not implemented under Alternative B and the Proposed RMP.  The resulting severity 
of adverse impacts would vary.  Alternatives A and C do not include implementation of 
the conservation strategies; therefore, these alternatives would not affect the hazardous 
materials and AML programs. 
Transportation and Access 
Route designations can have an indirect impact on hazardous materials because of the 
potential for illegal dumping.  Routes designated as open, particularly in remote 
locations, can attract illegal dumping activity.  Since Alternative A has no motorized use 
restrictions, this alternative represents the potentially most adverse impacts related to 
illegal dumping of hazardous materials.  Alternative B and the Proposed RMP contain the 
most restrictive motorized route designations and, therefore, represent the alternatives 
with the least potential to result in adverse impacts from illegal dumping.  Alternative C 
would be intermediate between Alternative A and the other two alternatives.  
4.18.4 Cumulative Impacts 
The cumulative impacts under all alternatives would benefit public safety and the 
environment by controlling or eliminating the potential for contaminants to migrate to 
surface soils, surface water, and groundwater.  Cumulative impacts from hazardous 
materials on specific resources such as water quality or soils are addressed in those 
sections.

ACECs 
Alternatives A and C would maintain the six existing ACECs.  No additional ACECs 
would be designated.  Therefore, values for which other alternatives have proposed new 
ACECs and RNAs would receive less protection.         
Alternative B proposes the largest increase in ACEC acreage. As a result, the 
designations would protect important environmental resources, including habitat for 
special status species, paleontological resources, and rare soils.  The designations would

Under the Proposed RMP, six existing ACECs would be maintained, seven new ones 
would be designated, and three ACECs would be expanded.  The benefits would be 
similar to Alternative B, except that important resources (special status plants) in the 
Yuba Brownsville area would not receive the same management attention/protection

BLM proposes various use restrictions for existing and proposed ACECs.  Restrictions 
proposed for the Pine Hill Preserve and Red Hills ACECs (Alternative B and the 
Proposed RMP) address camping, motorized use, land use authorizations (i.e., ROWs, 
R&PP Act leases, etc.), grazing, and other activities that could damage ACEC values.  
ROW/road construction in the Pine Hill Preserve is a particular threat to special status 
species.  Development of Wild Chaparral Road would destroy rare plant populations in 
the Preserve, take away lands that have been set aside for conservation, and interfere with 
local, state, and federal conservation goals for rare plant habitat.  Funds to acquire this 
parcel were contributed by USFWS, USBR, National Fish and Wildlife Foundation, and 
the Wildlife Conservation Board.  All these agencies donated their funds with the express 
understanding that the land purchased would be used for the conservation of five 
federally and state listed species and the habitat on which they depend.  To use the land 
for another purpose that would involve the destruction of large numbers of plants of these 
species, and the permanent destruction of their habitat would violate the intent under 
which the funds were donated.

4.19.4 Cumulative Impacts 
Because BLM lands are intermixed with private and other ownerships, beneficial 
cumulative impacts would result on non-BLM lands from special designations.  All 
alternatives would manage or improve areas with special designations.  Because plant 
and animal communities do not distinguish between BLM land and private land, any 
improved habitat protection would be expected to have cumulative beneficial impacts on 
habitat nearby, regardless of ownership.  Although Alternatives A and C would have 
beneficial cumulative impacts, Alternative B and the Proposed RMP would have the 
greatest beneficial cumulative impacts because they propose the most special 
designations.   
Other agencies, particularly the USFS, manage some of the same biological resources and 
rivers that occur on BLM land.  These agencies also benefit these resources through 
retention and improvement.  Residential development on private land would likely have 
an adverse impact on proposed wild and scenic river corridors and on outstanding 
biological resources that occur on those lands, increasing the importance of BLM land 
with special designations.

4.20 
Social and Economic Impacts (Including 
Environmental Justice) 
4.20.1 Introduction 
Refer to Section 3.20 for a description of the existing social and economic conditions in 
the planning area.  There is no BLM social/economic program.  The proposed actions 
under the various programs may impact social and economic conditions in the planning 
area are addressed below. 
4.20.2 Impacts of BLM Programs’ Proposed Actions on Social and 
Economic Conditions 
Lands and Realty  
Land Ownership Adjustment 
The principal social and economic impacts caused by the Sierra RMP may arise from 
BLM’s role as a large regional landowner, with over 1,000 parcels dispersed throughout 
the heavily populated portions of the Sierra Nevada foothills.  These often small areas 
increasingly serve as open spaces that provide recreation, habitat viewshed buffers, and 
solitude.  BLM parcels affect residents’ quality of life and may allow these residents to 
retain a sense of place that is threatened elsewhere in the region.  At the same time, BLM 
lands may adversely impact quality of life when public land abuses (squatting, 
irresponsible shooting, illegal off-road OHV use, illegal campfires, etc.) disrupt adjacent 
private landowners’ enjoyment of their own property and may even affect land values. 
BLM land ownership adjustment, as proposed under all of the alternatives, could have 
beneficial social and economic impacts.  Adjustment to resolve trespass, improve access, 
allow public facilities (under R&PP Act lease), expand public ownership of significant 
biological habitat, or consolidate ownership (thus improving general management) would 
all enhance the social and economic benefits described above.  To some extent, 
individual property owners may lose access to or enjoyment of parcels adjacent to their 
property because of land ownership adjustments.  However, entire communities may gain 
from having larger, more accessible blocks of BLM land in popular, scenic areas.  
The alternatives differ in the amount of land ownership adjustment anticipated.  
Alternative A would continue current land ownership adjustment patterns, which tend to 
involve following opportunities as they arise on a case-by-case basis.  Alternative B 
would focus on preserving and protecting sensitive resources, such as special 
designations and critical habitat for special status species.  This alternative would do 
more to affect those who feel their quality of life is associated with increased open space, 
environmental protection, and ecosystem and habitat improvement, and would not so 
much benefit those who value recreational opportunities.  Alternative C would improve 
access to SRMAs and would expand these areas.  This alternative would also authorize 
disposals to counties, through the R&PP Act, for facilities to enhance recreation area 
development.  Acquisitions would focus on high-quality recreation land rather than

Mineral Withdrawals 
Under Alternative B and the Proposed RMP, some BLM land would be recommended for 
mineral withdrawal, which would reduce opportunities for locatable mineral

high.   
Recreation (Target Shooting) 
Target shooting is becoming increasingly controversial as residential development 
adjacent to BLM land increases.  BLM frequently receives complaints from neighbors 
regarding target shooting.  Shooting has been cited by many as a negative social 
consequence of living adjacent to BLM land.  On the other hand, there a number of 
people who enjoy target shooting on public land.  BLM lands offer, in some cases, easily 
accessible, no-cost places to shoot.  
All alternatives limit target shooting in high use recreation areas (SRMAs in Alternatives 
B, C, and the Proposed RMP).  Target shooting would be permitted unless signed closed 
outside these high use areas (Alternative B would prohibit target shooting in the North 
Fork American SRMA).  Refer to the recreation section (4.15) for an analysis of impacts 
caused by these restrictions.  All alternatives would likely continue to result in complaints 
from neighbors about shooting.  There would be minor and sometimes moderate adverse 
impacts on social conditions.  The impacts to shooters would be unchanged from current 
impacts, except under Alternative B in the North Fork American SRMA where they 
would be adversely impacted by being prohibited from shooting.    
Transportation and Access (Motorized Vehicle/OHV Use Designations) 
Under Alternative A, all BLM land would be open to motorized use except where closed.  
Due to BLM’s scattered land ownership pattern in the planning area, trespass is a 
significant problem.  BLM manages many small tracts of public land.  Often these tracts 
are entirely surrounded by private property.  Routes of travel cross public land, then 
return to private property.  Many routes are not public roads.  Trespass is inevitable 
because motorized users are often unaware of public land boundaries and do not have 
permission to drive on private lands.  This problem has resulted in numerous complaints 
and affects the quality of life for property owners adjacent to public lands.   
Alternative A would continue the current management of motorized use and would, 
therefore, not adequately address the trespass problem, resulting in continued impacts to 
BLM’s neighbors.  At the same time, BLM’s current management makes the public lands 
readily accessible to motorized users, enhancing their quality of life.

Under Alternative C, motorized use would be limited to existing routes that have not 
been closed.  Under Alternative B and the Proposed RMP, motorized use would be

BLM land, especially developed recreation areas.  Alternative B would have the fewest 
routes available for motorized use.  
Alternative B and the Proposed RMP would have the most positive impact on trespass-

Special Designations  
Wild and Scenic Rivers 
Under Alternative A, no additional rivers in the planning area would be recommended as 
suitable for wild and scenic designation.  This alternative would allow for the potential 
construction of dams/reservoirs on rivers determined eligible and suitable for wild and 
scenic status under other alternatives.  At this time, there appears to be no substantive 
demand that would make construction of new dams or water diversions on these rivers 
economically feasible.   
Under Alternative B, seven rivers would be recommended as eligible and suitable for 
wild and scenic river designation.  This would be beneficial to those who value these 
rivers and to those who live along the rivers and feel their quality of life is enhanced by 
the rivers’ wild and scenic qualities.  There is considerable evidence that proximity to 
rivers, greenways, and other natural amenities enhances property values.  Designating 
these rivers as wild and scenic could increase or help maintain adjacent and nearby 
property values.  The locally and seasonally important commercial rafting industry would 
also benefit, especially from the protection of the South Fork American River, one of the 
most popular white water rivers in the country.  
The social impacts would be adverse if these rivers were dammed or lost their free-
flowing condition as a result of a major water project.  Economically, the impacts of this 
are unclear.  The thriving white water rafting industry on the South Fork would be 
destroyed.  On the other hand, such a water project could benefit the local economy, at 
least during construction, and, over the long term, provide water and energy at reduced 
costs to Californians.  It could also prevent flooding downstream in the Central Valley, 
especially in Sacramento.  The threat of flooding in the Central Valley lowlands is very 
real.  Flooding is checked by several major reservoirs, including Pardee and Camanche 
on the Mokelumne River, and Folsom and Natomas on the American River.  Taxpayers’ 
dollars are best spent on projects designed to shore up and repair the levy system.  
Alternative B could, pending congressional action, prevent the construction of new dams 
and other major water projects in the proposed wild and scenic river corridors.  However, 
if future water requirements and/or energy needs in California were to create such
